# How to use this guide

Pathophysiology is a "story" subject: every disease follows the same chain — **cause → mechanism → what you see → what can go wrong**. Study one unit at a time: read the notes, draw each flow diagram once from memory, learn the comparison tables, then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short answer (5-mark) and long essay (10-mark) questions, rated by how often that kind of question appears in PCI-syllabus pharmacy papers.

The five units here follow the five units of the PCI syllabus. Unit 1 is large because the syllabus puts cell injury, acid–base and electrolytes, inflammation, wound healing and atherosclerosis together in it; read it over two days. Atherosclerosis is explained fully in Unit 1 (where the syllabus first names it) and only summarised again under ischaemic heart disease in Unit 2.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ questions | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with a flow diagram and a comparison table.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Cell injury and inflammation | Causes and mechanism of cell injury, adaptive changes, apoptosis vs necrosis, acidosis and alkalosis, mechanism of inflammation and its mediators, wound healing, atherosclerosis |
| 2 CVS, respiratory, renal | Hypertension, congestive heart failure, angina and myocardial infarction, asthma, COPD, acute and chronic renal failure |
| 3 Blood, endocrine, CNS, GI | Anaemias (iron, B12/folate, sickle cell, thalassaemia), haemophilia, diabetes mellitus, thyroid disorders, epilepsy, Parkinson's, stroke, depression, schizophrenia, Alzheimer's, peptic ulcer |
| 4 Liver, joints, cancer | Crohn's vs ulcerative colitis, types of jaundice, hepatitis viruses, alcoholic liver disease, rheumatoid arthritis, osteoporosis, gout, benign vs malignant tumours, carcinogenesis |
| 5 Infections and STDs | Tuberculosis, typhoid, leprosy, meningitis, UTI, AIDS, syphilis, gonorrhoea |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Use the same skeleton for every disease answer: **Definition → Aetiology/risk factors → Pathogenesis (flow diagram) → Signs and symptoms → Complications → Diagnosis (one line)**. Examiners mark against these headings.
2. Draw a flow chart for pathogenesis (arrows from cause to effect). It earns marks quickly and shows you understand the mechanism.
3. "Differentiate" questions are frequent: learn the tables — apoptosis vs necrosis, acute vs chronic inflammation, exudate vs transudate, dystrophic vs metastatic calcification, type 1 vs type 2 diabetes, Crohn's vs UC, three types of jaundice, benign vs malignant tumour, tuberculoid vs lepromatous leprosy, left vs right heart failure, asthma vs COPD, acute vs chronic renal failure.
4. Give real Indian examples where they fit: hookworm and diet in iron deficiency, hepatitis E epidemics, gutka in oral cancer, TB and leprosy burden.
5. Learn the key numbers: pH 7.35–7.45, Na⁺ 135–145, K⁺ 3.5–5.0 mEq/L, BP 140/90, fasting glucose 126 mg/dL, HbA1c 6.5%, Hb 13/12 g/dL, CD4 < 200 cells/µL, T-score −2.5, oliguria < 400 ml/day, CKD GFR < 60 for > 3 months, visible jaundice at 2–3 mg/dL bilirubin.
6. Link to drugs in one line at the end where it helps (e.g. NSAIDs block COX, steroids block phospholipase A2, levodopa replaces dopamine in Parkinson's) — this subject is the base for pharmacology.
7. Spellings matter: aetiology, haemoglobin, oedema, ischaemia, diarrhoea; and write organism names in full the first time (*Mycobacterium tuberculosis*).

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five topics with a flow diagram each: **mechanism of inflammation with mediators**, **cell injury (causes, mechanism, adaptations, necrosis vs apoptosis)**, **hypertension or congestive heart failure**, **diabetes mellitus**, and **tuberculosis**. Then revise the comparison tables below — they cover most short questions.

**Unit 1 in ten lines**

- Homeostasis = negative feedback (temperature, BP, glucose); positive feedback = labour, clotting.
- Cell injury: hypoxia is the commonest cause → ATP loss → Na⁺ pump fails → swelling → Ca²⁺ influx, free radicals, membrane damage → necrosis.
- Atrophy ↓ size · hypertrophy ↑ size · hyperplasia ↑ number · metaplasia = cell type change · dysplasia = disordered, pre-cancerous.
- Necrosis types: coagulative (heart), liquefactive (brain, abscess), caseous (TB), fat (pancreas), fibrinoid, gangrene.
- Apoptosis: shrinkage, caspases, no inflammation.
- Dystrophic calcification = dead tissue, normal Ca; metastatic = normal tissue, high Ca.
- Inflammation signs: rubor, calor, tumor, dolor, functio laesa.
- WBC: margination → rolling (selectins) → adhesion (integrins/ICAM-1) → diapedesis → chemotaxis → phagocytosis.
- Wound healing: haemostasis → inflammation → proliferation (granulation tissue) → remodelling.
- Atherosclerosis: endothelial injury → oxidised LDL → foam cells → fatty streak → fibrous plaque → rupture → thrombus.

**Numbers worth memorising**

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Arterial pH / HCO3⁻ / PaCO2 | 7.35–7.45 / 22–26 mEq/L / 35–45 mmHg |
| Serum Na⁺ / K⁺ | 135–145 / 3.5–5.0 mEq/L |
| Anion gap | Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO3⁻) ≈ 8–12 mEq/L |
| Hypertension | ≥ 140/90 mmHg |
| Diabetes | FPG ≥ 126 mg/dL; 2-h OGTT ≥ 200; HbA1c ≥ 6.5% |
| Anaemia (WHO) | Hb < 13 g/dL men, < 12 women, < 11 pregnancy |
| Oliguria | < 400 ml/day |
| CKD | GFR < 60 ml/min/1.73 m² for > 3 months |
| Visible jaundice | Bilirubin about 2–3 mg/dL |
| Urate saturation | About 6.8 mg/dL |
| Osteoporosis | T-score ≤ −2.5 |
| AIDS | CD4 < 200 cells/µL |
| Significant bacteriuria | ≥ 10⁵ CFU/ml |
| TB suspect | Cough ≥ 2 weeks |

**Must-know comparisons**

| Pair | One-line difference |
| --- | --- |
| Acute vs chronic inflammation | Neutrophils, fast, little fibrosis vs macrophages/lymphocytes, slow, fibrosis |
| Exudate vs transudate | Protein-rich, SG > 1.020 vs protein-poor, SG < 1.012 |
| Primary vs secondary intention | Clean, close edges, thin scar vs gaping wound, granulation, contraction |
| Left vs right heart failure | Lungs (dyspnoea, orthopnoea, crackles) vs body veins (oedema, JVP, liver) |
| Stable vs unstable vs Prinzmetal angina | Exertion vs rest (plaque rupture) vs spasm |
| Asthma vs COPD | Young, IgE, eosinophils, reversible vs smoker, neutrophils, poorly reversible |
| Chronic bronchitis vs emphysema | Productive cough 3 months × 2 years vs alveolar wall destruction |
| Acute vs chronic renal failure | Sudden, reversible vs slow, irreversible, anaemia, bone disease |
| B12 vs folate deficiency | Nerve damage, pernicious anaemia vs no nerve damage, pregnancy, drugs |
| Haemophilia A vs B | Factor VIII vs factor IX (both X-linked recessive) |
| Type 1 vs type 2 diabetes | Autoimmune, thin, ketoacidosis, insulin vs insulin resistance, obese, oral drugs |
| Hyper- vs hypothyroidism | Weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia vs weight gain, cold intolerance, bradycardia |
| Gastric vs duodenal ulcer | Pain after food, weight loss vs pain relieved by food, night pain |
| Crohn's vs UC | Skip, transmural, granulomas, fistulae vs continuous from rectum, mucosal, bloody diarrhoea |
| Jaundice types | Haemolytic (unconjugated) · hepatocellular (both) · obstructive (conjugated, pale stools, itch) |
| RA vs osteoarthritis | Autoimmune, small joints, symmetrical, long morning stiffness vs wear-and-tear, weight-bearing joints |
| Benign vs malignant | Capsule, no invasion or metastasis vs invasion, metastasis, anaplasia |
| Tuberculoid vs lepromatous leprosy | Good immunity, few bacilli, few anaesthetic patches vs poor immunity, many bacilli, leonine face |
| Primary vs secondary TB | Ghon complex, children vs apical cavity, reactivation in adults |

**Key mechanisms in one line**

| Disease | Core mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Hypertension | ↑ CO × ↑ TPR via RAAS, sympathetic activity, Na⁺ retention |
| Heart failure | ↓ output → SNS + RAAS + ADH + remodelling (help, then harm) |
| MI | Plaque rupture → occlusive thrombus → necrosis after ~20–40 min |
| Asthma | Th2 → IgE → mast cells → early (histamine, LTs) and late (eosinophils) phase |
| Emphysema | Protease (elastase) > antiprotease (α1-antitrypsin) |
| Sickle cell | Glu → Val at β6 → HbS polymerises at low O2 |
| Parkinson's | Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine neurons, Lewy bodies (α-synuclein) |
| Alzheimer's | β-amyloid plaques + tau tangles + ACh loss |
| Schizophrenia | Mesolimbic dopamine excess (positive symptoms) |
| Depression | Monoamine (NA, 5-HT) deficit, HPA overactivity |
| Peptic ulcer | H. pylori and NSAIDs tip acid/pepsin over mucosal defence |
| Gout | Urate crystals → IL-1β inflammation; podagra |
| Cancer | Oncogenes on (RAS, MYC) + suppressors off (p53, RB) + no apoptosis |
| HIV | gp120 + CD4 + CCR5/CXCR4 → reverse transcriptase → CD4 loss |

**Organisms in one line**: TB — *M. tuberculosis*; leprosy — *M. leprae*; typhoid — *Salmonella* Typhi; UTI — *E. coli*; meningitis — pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib; syphilis — *Treponema pallidum*; gonorrhoea — *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*; AIDS — HIV (retrovirus); peptic ulcer and gastric cancer — *Helicobacter pylori*; cervical cancer — HPV.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: cell injury is the set of changes produced in a cell when stress exceeds its ability to adapt; it may be reversible or end in cell death.
2. Causes: hypoxia/ischaemia (most common), physical agents (trauma, heat, cold, radiation, electricity), chemicals and drugs (cyanide, CCl4, paracetamol overdose, alcohol), infectious agents, immunological reactions, genetic defects, nutritional imbalance, ageing.
3. ATP depletion: loss of oxidative phosphorylation → Na+/K+-ATPase fails → Na+ and water enter → cell swelling; anaerobic glycolysis → lactic acid → low pH; ribosomes detach → less protein synthesis.
4. Mitochondrial damage: permeability transition pores open, cytochrome c leaks → apoptosis; more free radicals.
5. Calcium influx: raised cytosolic Ca2+ activates phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases, ATPases.
6. Free radicals (superoxide, H2O2, hydroxyl): lipid peroxidation of membranes, protein cross-linking, DNA breaks; important in reperfusion injury.
7. Membrane damage: loss of permeability; lysosomal enzymes leak and digest the cell; enzymes leak into blood (ALT, troponin).
8. DNA and protein damage → apoptosis if not repaired.
9. Flow: ↓O2 → ↓ATP → swelling (reversible) → continued hypoxia → membrane + mitochondrial damage + Ca2+ → necrosis (irreversible).
10. Reversible: cell swelling, fatty change, blebs, ER swelling, ribosome detachment. Irreversible: severe mitochondrial damage, membrane rupture, nuclear changes (pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis).
questions.question: Define cell injury. Describe the causes and the mechanism (pathogenesis) of cell injury, and distinguish reversible from irreversible injury.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: protective response of vascularised tissue to injury that removes the cause and dead tissue and starts repair. Cardinal signs: rubor, calor, tumor, dolor, functio laesa.
2. Vascular events: brief arteriolar vasoconstriction → vasodilatation (histamine, NO, PGs) → increased blood flow (redness, heat) → increased permeability (endothelial contraction in venules, direct injury, leukocyte injury, transcytosis, leaky new vessels) → protein-rich exudate (swelling) → stasis.
3. Exudate vs transudate: protein-rich, SG above 1.020 vs protein-poor, SG below 1.012.
4. Cellular events: margination → rolling (selectins) → firm adhesion (integrins with ICAM-1/VCAM-1, induced by TNF and IL-1) → transmigration/diapedesis (PECAM-1) → chemotaxis (C5a, LTB4, IL-8, bacterial products) → phagocytosis (opsonisation by C3b and IgG, engulfment, killing by reactive oxygen species and myeloperoxidase, digestion).
5. Neutrophils first 6–24 h, then macrophages after 24–48 h.
6. Mediators: histamine and serotonin (vasodilatation, permeability); prostaglandins (vasodilatation, pain, fever); thromboxane A2 (vasoconstriction, platelet aggregation); leukotrienes (LTB4 chemotaxis; LTC4/D4/E4 bronchoconstriction, permeability); PAF; cytokines TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6 (fever, endothelial activation, acute-phase proteins); chemokines (IL-8); nitric oxide; complement (C3a/C5a anaphylatoxins, C5a chemotaxis, C3b opsonin, C5b–9 lysis); bradykinin (pain, permeability).
7. Arachidonic acid pathway: phospholipase A2 (blocked by steroids) → COX (blocked by NSAIDs) → PGs and TXA2; 5-lipoxygenase → leukotrienes.
8. Outcomes: resolution, fibrosis, abscess, chronic inflammation.
questions.question: What is inflammation? Describe the vascular and cellular events of acute inflammation and list the chemical mediators with their actions.

questions.answer:
1. Repair = regeneration (same cells) + fibrosis (scar).
2. Phases: haemostasis (platelet plug, fibrin clot scaffold); inflammation (days 1–3: neutrophils then macrophages; growth factors PDGF, TGF-β, VEGF, FGF); proliferation (days 3–14: granulation tissue of new capillaries and fibroblasts, re-epithelialisation, type III collagen, myofibroblast contraction); maturation/remodelling (weeks–months: type III → type I collagen, pale scar, strength rises but never reaches normal).
3. First intention: clean surgical wound, edges close, little granulation tissue, minimal contraction, thin scar, quick, low infection risk.
4. Second intention: large gaping or infected wound with tissue loss, abundant granulation tissue from the base, marked wound contraction, large scar, slow.
5. Local factors: infection (most important), poor blood supply, foreign body, movement, pressure, radiation, large size.
6. Systemic factors: malnutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc), diabetes, corticosteroids, old age, anaemia, poor circulation, chemotherapy.
7. Complications: infection, dehiscence, hypertrophic scar, keloid, contracture, incisional hernia.
questions.question: Describe the basic principles of wound healing in the skin. Compare healing by first and second intention and list the factors affecting healing.

questions.answer:
1. Atrophy: decrease in cell size — thymus after puberty; muscle wasting after denervation or immobilisation.
2. Hypertrophy: increase in cell size — uterus in pregnancy, left ventricle in hypertension.
3. Hyperplasia: increase in cell number — breast in lactation, endometrial hyperplasia, benign prostatic hyperplasia.
4. Metaplasia: one adult cell type replaced by another — columnar to squamous in smokers' bronchi; squamous to columnar in Barrett's oesophagus.
5. Dysplasia: disordered growth with variation in size and shape and large dark nuclei — cervix; pre-cancerous.
6. Adaptations are usually reversible when the stimulus is removed; dysplasia may progress to cancer.
questions.question: Write a note on cellular adaptations with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Nature: programmed, controlled vs accidental, uncontrolled.
2. Extent: single cells vs groups of cells.
3. Cell size: shrinks vs swells.
4. Membrane: intact, apoptotic bodies vs ruptured.
5. Nucleus: chromatin condensation and fragmentation vs pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis.
6. Inflammation: none vs present.
7. Enzymes: caspases vs lysosomal enzymes.
8. Examples: embryonic development, removal of virus-infected or DNA-damaged cells vs infarction, burns, toxins.
questions.question: Differentiate between apoptosis and necrosis.

questions.answer:
1. Normal arterial pH 7.35–7.45; HCO3- 22–26 mEq/L.
2. Metabolic acidosis: primary fall in HCO3-. Causes: diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure, severe diarrhoea, methanol or salicylate poisoning.
3. Anion gap = Na+ − (Cl- + HCO3-), about 8–12; raised with added acids, normal with bicarbonate loss (diarrhoea).
4. Compensation: hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing) lowers PaCO2.
5. Effects: weak heart contraction, hypotension, confusion, hyperkalaemia.
6. Metabolic alkalosis: primary rise in HCO3-. Causes: vomiting, nasogastric suction, diuretics, excess antacids, hypokalaemia.
7. Compensation: hypoventilation raises PaCO2. Effects: tingling, tetany (low ionised Ca2+), arrhythmias.
questions.question: Explain metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis with causes and compensation.

questions.answer:
1. Risk factors: age, male sex, family history; high LDL, hypertension, smoking, diabetes, obesity, inactivity, low HDL.
2. Endothelial injury/dysfunction → increased permeability and adhesion molecules.
3. LDL enters intima and is oxidised.
4. Monocytes enter, become macrophages and take up oxidised LDL → foam cells → fatty streak.
5. Growth factors (PDGF) make smooth muscle cells migrate to intima, multiply and lay down collagen → fibrous cap over lipid core = atheroma.
6. Complicated plaque: calcification, ulceration, rupture, thrombosis, haemorrhage.
7. Complications: angina, MI, stroke, peripheral gangrene, aneurysm, embolism.
questions.question: Describe the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis and its complications.

questions.answer:
1. Dystrophic: in dead or degenerating tissue; serum calcium normal; atheroma, damaged valves, TB caseous necrosis, fat necrosis.
2. Metastatic: in normal tissue; hypercalcaemia; hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D excess, bone-destroying tumours, renal failure; sites kidney, lung, stomach, vessels.
3. Accumulations: lipids (fatty liver), cholesterol (foam cells), proteins (Russell bodies, Mallory bodies), glycogen (diabetes), exogenous pigment (carbon — anthracosis), endogenous pigments (lipofuscin, melanin, haemosiderin, bilirubin).
questions.question: Differentiate dystrophic and metastatic calcification, and list common intracellular accumulations.

questions.answer: Rubor (redness), calor (heat), tumor (swelling), dolor (pain) — described by Celsus — and functio laesa (loss of function), added by Virchow.
questions.question: List the cardinal signs of inflammation.

questions.answer: Negative: body temperature regulation, baroreceptor control of blood pressure (also blood glucose by insulin/glucagon). Positive: oxytocin and uterine contractions in labour, blood clotting cascade.
questions.question: Give two examples each of negative and positive feedback.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: persistent rise of arterial BP; diagnosed at 140/90 mmHg or above on repeated readings; normal below 120/80.
2. Classification: stage 1 (140–159/90–99), stage 2 (160/100 or more); primary/essential (90–95%) and secondary.
3. Secondary causes: renal (CKD, renal artery stenosis), endocrine (Conn's, Cushing's, phaeochromocytoma, hyperthyroidism), coarctation of aorta, pregnancy, drugs (oral contraceptives, steroids, NSAIDs).
4. Pathogenesis: BP = cardiac output × peripheral resistance.
5. RAAS: low renal perfusion → renin → angiotensin I → ACE → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction, aldosterone (Na+/water retention), ADH, thirst.
6. Sympathetic overactivity: raised heart rate, contractility, vasoconstriction, renin.
7. Sodium retention and high salt intake; endothelial dysfunction (less NO, more endothelin); vascular remodelling; obesity, insulin resistance, genetics, ageing.
8. Clinical features: usually silent; occipital morning headache, dizziness, palpitations, epistaxis, blurred vision.
9. Complications: heart (LVH, failure, IHD), brain (stroke, encephalopathy), kidney (nephrosclerosis, CKD), eye (retinopathy), vessels (atherosclerosis, aortic dissection); hypertensive crisis.
questions.question: Define hypertension. Classify it and discuss its pathogenesis, clinical features and complications.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: the heart cannot pump enough blood for tissue needs, or does so only at high filling pressures, with congestion.
2. Causes: ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, valve disease, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, arrhythmias, congenital disease; high-output states (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis).
3. Precipitating factors: infection, uncontrolled BP, non-adherence, salt/fluid excess, NSAIDs.
4. Types: systolic vs diastolic; left vs right; acute vs chronic; low vs high output.
5. Compensation: low output → sympathetic activation (tachycardia, vasoconstriction), RAAS (salt and water retention), ADH, Frank–Starling mechanism, ventricular hypertrophy and remodelling; useful at first but increase preload, afterload and workload → vicious cycle.
6. Left failure: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, cough, frothy sputum, basal crackles, pulmonary oedema, fatigue.
7. Right failure: pitting ankle oedema, raised JVP, enlarged liver, ascites, anorexia; cor pulmonale when due to lung disease.
8. NYHA classes I–IV.
9. Complications: pulmonary oedema, arrhythmias, sudden death, renal failure, thromboembolism, cachexia.
questions.question: Define congestive heart failure. Describe its causes, pathophysiology (compensatory mechanisms) and the features of left and right heart failure.

questions.answer:
1. IHD: imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand; over 90% due to coronary atherosclerosis.
2. Forms: angina, acute MI, chronic IHD, sudden cardiac death.
3. Stable angina: fixed narrowing, pain on exertion, relieved by rest or nitrate.
4. Unstable angina: plaque rupture with non-occlusive thrombus, pain at rest or crescendo, high MI risk.
5. Prinzmetal angina: coronary spasm, pain at rest, transient ST elevation.
6. MI pathogenesis: plaque rupture → platelet adhesion and aggregation (TXA2, ADP) → coagulation → occlusive thrombus → ATP loss → irreversible injury after about 20–40 min → necrosis spreads subendocardium to full thickness.
7. Types: transmural (STEMI), subendocardial (NSTEMI).
8. Features: crushing retrosternal pain > 20–30 min not relieved by nitrates, radiating to arm/jaw; sweating, nausea, breathlessness, anxiety; silent MI in diabetics and elderly.
9. Diagnosis: ECG (ST elevation, Q waves), troponin I/T (most specific), CK-MB.
10. Complications: arrhythmias (VF), heart failure, cardiogenic shock, rupture, aneurysm, pericarditis, mural thrombus and embolism.
questions.question: Describe ischaemic heart disease. Discuss the types of angina and the pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications of myocardial infarction.

questions.answer:
1. Chronic airway inflammation with reversible obstruction and hyper-responsiveness.
2. Types: extrinsic (allergic, IgE) and intrinsic; drug-induced (aspirin, β-blockers), occupational, exercise-induced.
3. Sensitisation: allergen → Th2 cells → IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 → IgE binds mast cells.
4. Early phase: mast cell degranulation → histamine, LTC4/D4/E4, PGD2 → bronchospasm, oedema, mucus.
5. Late phase (4–8 h): eosinophils, Th2 cells → inflammation, epithelial damage.
6. Remodelling: smooth muscle hypertrophy, thick basement membrane, goblet cell hyperplasia.
7. Features: episodic wheeze, dyspnoea, chest tightness, night cough, prolonged expiration, low PEF improving with bronchodilator.
8. Complications: status asthmaticus, respiratory failure, pneumothorax.
questions.question: Describe the pathogenesis and clinical features of bronchial asthma.

questions.answer:
1. Persistent, poorly reversible airflow limitation; post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70.
2. Causes: cigarette smoking (main), biomass smoke, pollution, α1-antitrypsin deficiency.
3. Chronic bronchitis: productive cough at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years; mucus gland hypertrophy, goblet cell hyperplasia; cyanosis, oedema (blue bloater).
4. Emphysema: permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to terminal bronchiole with wall destruction; protease–antiprotease imbalance (neutrophil elastase vs α1-antitrypsin); loss of elastic recoil; pursed lips, barrel chest (pink puffer).
5. Centriacinar (smokers, upper lobes) vs panacinar (α1-antitrypsin deficiency, lower lobes).
6. Complications: exacerbations, respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, polycythaemia, pneumothorax.
questions.question: Write a note on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (chronic bronchitis and emphysema).

questions.answer:
1. Onset: sudden (hours–days) vs slow (months–years).
2. Reversibility: often reversible vs irreversible, progressive.
3. Causes: pre-renal (dehydration, shock), renal (acute tubular necrosis, nephrotoxic drugs), post-renal (obstruction) vs diabetes, hypertension, chronic glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney.
4. Definition: rapid rise of creatinine, oliguria < 400 ml/day vs GFR < 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 for > 3 months.
5. Kidney size: normal vs usually small and scarred.
6. Anaemia (low erythropoietin) and renal osteodystrophy: absent vs present.
7. Phases: oliguric, diuretic, recovery vs stages 1–5 ending in ESRD needing dialysis.
8. Both: hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload, uraemia; reduce doses of renally cleared drugs.
questions.question: Differentiate acute renal failure from chronic renal failure.

questions.answer:
1. Fluid overload, oedema and hypertension (salt and water retention).
2. Hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis (reduced excretion of K+ and H+).
3. Normocytic anaemia — lack of erythropoietin.
4. Renal osteodystrophy — less 1-α hydroxylation of vitamin D, phosphate retention, hypocalcaemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism.
5. Uraemia — nausea, itching, confusion, pericarditis, neuropathy.
6. Cardiovascular disease — LVH, heart failure, atherosclerosis (main cause of death).
7. Bleeding tendency, infections, altered drug handling.
questions.question: Describe the complications of chronic kidney disease and their causes.

questions.answer:
1. Arteriosclerosis: general term for thickening and loss of elasticity (hardening) of arterial walls.
2. Forms: atherosclerosis, Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis, arteriolosclerosis (hyaline and hyperplastic).
3. Atherosclerosis: lipid-rich intimal plaques in large and medium arteries; narrows lumen; causes MI, stroke, gangrene.
4. Mönckeberg: calcium in media of medium arteries of elderly; no narrowing.
5. Arteriolosclerosis: small arteries/arterioles; hyaline in hypertension and diabetes; onion-skin in malignant hypertension.
6. All atherosclerosis is arteriosclerosis, but not vice versa.
questions.question: Differentiate arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis.

questions.answer: Breathlessness on lying flat, relieved by sitting up. It indicates left heart failure: lying down returns more blood to the congested lungs.
questions.question: What is orthopnoea and what does it indicate?

questions.answer: Cardiac troponin (I or T); it rises within a few hours and stays raised for about 1–2 weeks.
questions.question: Name the most specific blood marker for myocardial infarction.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: metabolic disorder with chronic hyperglycaemia from defective insulin secretion, action or both.
2. Diagnosis: FPG ≥ 126 mg/dL, 2-h OGTT ≥ 200, HbA1c ≥ 6.5%, or random ≥ 200 with symptoms.
3. Classification: type 1, type 2, gestational, other (pancreatitis, Cushing's, steroids).
4. Type 1: autoimmune T-cell destruction of β-cells (antibodies to GAD, islets) in genetically prone people, viral trigger; absolute insulin deficiency; young, thin, sudden onset, ketoacidosis; 5–10%.
5. Type 2: insulin resistance (muscle, fat, liver) plus progressive β-cell failure; obesity, inactivity, family history; adults, slow onset; about 90%.
6. Symptoms: hyperglycaemia → glycosuria above renal threshold (about 180 mg/dL) → osmotic diuresis → polyuria, polydipsia; polyphagia, weight loss, fatigue, infections, slow healing.
7. Acute complications: DKA (ketones, acidosis, Kussmaul breathing), hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, hypoglycaemia.
8. Chronic microvascular: retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy. Macrovascular: coronary disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease.
9. Others: diabetic foot, infections, cataract.
10. Mechanisms of damage: protein glycation (AGEs), sorbitol pathway, oxidative stress.
questions.question: Define diabetes mellitus. Classify it and discuss the pathogenesis, clinical features and complications of type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

questions.answer:
1. Anaemia: Hb below 13 g/dL (men), 12 (women), 11 (pregnancy).
2. Classification by MCV: microcytic hypochromic (iron deficiency, thalassaemia), normocytic (blood loss, CKD, aplastic, haemolytic), macrocytic (B12, folate). By cause: blood loss, decreased production, increased destruction.
3. Iron deficiency causes: chronic blood loss (menorrhagia, hookworm, ulcer, piles, NSAIDs), increased need (pregnancy, growth), poor intake, malabsorption.
4. Pathogenesis: stores (ferritin) fall → serum iron falls, TIBC rises → haem synthesis fails → small pale cells.
5. Features: fatigue, pallor, koilonychia, glossitis, angular stomatitis, pica. Blood: low Hb, MCV, MCH, low ferritin, high TIBC.
6. Megaloblastic: B12 or folate lack impairs DNA synthesis → nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony → megaloblasts, macrocytes, ineffective erythropoiesis.
7. B12 causes: pernicious anaemia (no intrinsic factor), vegan diet, gastrectomy, ileal disease. Folate causes: poor diet, pregnancy, alcohol, methotrexate, phenytoin.
8. B12 lack causes neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration); folate lack does not; folate needed to prevent neural tube defects.
9. Blood: raised MCV, oval macrocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils, raised LDH and bilirubin.
questions.question: Classify anaemias. Describe the causes, pathogenesis and blood picture of iron deficiency anaemia and megaloblastic anaemia.

questions.answer:
1. Parkinson's: progressive degenerative movement disorder of the elderly.
2. Pathogenesis: loss of dopaminergic neurons of substantia nigra pars compacta → low striatal dopamine, relative ACh excess; Lewy bodies of α-synuclein; oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, genes, toxins (MPTP, pesticides).
3. Features (TRAP): resting pill-rolling tremor, lead-pipe/cog-wheel rigidity, akinesia/bradykinesia (mask face, micrographia), postural instability with shuffling gait; non-motor: depression, constipation, anosmia, dementia.
4. Drug-induced parkinsonism: antipsychotics, metoclopramide.
5. Alzheimer's: commonest cause of dementia, usually after 65.
6. Pathology: extracellular β-amyloid plaques, intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau, neuron loss in hippocampus and cortex, brain atrophy; cholinergic deficit (nucleus basalis of Meynert).
7. Risk factors: age, family history, ApoE ε4, Down syndrome, head injury.
8. Features: loss of recent memory, disorientation, language problems, poor judgement, personality change, later total dependence.
questions.question: Describe the aetiology, pathogenesis and clinical features of Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease.

questions.answer:
1. Break in gastric or duodenal mucosa through muscularis mucosae due to acid and pepsin.
2. Aggressive factors: acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs, smoking, alcohol, Zollinger–Ellison syndrome.
3. Protective factors: mucus–bicarbonate layer, prostaglandins, blood flow, cell renewal.
4. H. pylori: urease makes ammonia, toxins and inflammation damage mucosa, raise gastrin and acid. NSAIDs block COX → less protective PG.
5. Duodenal ulcer: pain 2–3 h after meals and at night, relieved by food. Gastric: pain soon after food, weight loss.
6. Complications: haemorrhage (haematemesis, melaena), perforation, pyloric obstruction, malignancy (gastric).
questions.question: Describe the pathogenesis, clinical features and complications of peptic ulcer.

questions.answer:
1. Autosomal recessive; point mutation in β-globin gene: glutamic acid → valine at position 6 → HbS.
2. Low O2, dehydration, acidosis, infection → HbS polymerises → rigid sickle cells.
3. Sickle cells block small vessels → ischaemia, painful crises; and are destroyed early → haemolytic anaemia.
4. Features: chronic anaemia, jaundice, gallstones, bone/chest/abdominal pain, hand–foot syndrome, stroke, acute chest syndrome, leg ulcers, autosplenectomy and infections, aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19).
5. Trait (HbAS) usually symptom-free and partly protective against falciparum malaria.
questions.question: Write a note on sickle cell anaemia.

questions.answer:
1. Common cause: Graves' disease (TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies) vs Hashimoto's thyroiditis, iodine deficiency.
2. Metabolism: raised vs reduced.
3. Weight: loss despite good appetite vs gain.
4. Temperature: heat intolerance, sweating vs cold intolerance, dry skin.
5. Heart: tachycardia, atrial fibrillation vs bradycardia.
6. Bowel: diarrhoea vs constipation.
7. Nervous: tremor, anxiety vs slowness, depression, slow reflexes.
8. Special: exophthalmos vs myxoedema; cretinism in infants.
9. Tests: high T3/T4, low TSH vs low T4, high TSH (primary).
questions.question: Compare hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism.

questions.answer:
1. Inherited bleeding disorder from clotting factor deficiency.
2. Haemophilia A: factor VIII (more common); haemophilia B (Christmas disease): factor IX.
3. X-linked recessive: males affected, females carriers, no father-to-son transmission.
4. Features: easy bruising, prolonged bleeding after injury, dental extraction or surgery; haemarthrosis of knees, elbows, ankles leading to joint deformity; muscle and intracranial bleeds.
5. Tests: prolonged aPTT; normal PT, platelets, bleeding time; factor assay.
6. Avoid aspirin, NSAIDs and IM injections.
questions.question: Write a note on haemophilia.

questions.answer:
1. Seizure: sudden, excessive, synchronous neuronal discharge; epilepsy: recurrent unprovoked seizures.
2. Mechanism: imbalance between excitation (glutamate, Na+ and Ca2+ channels) and inhibition (GABA).
3. Causes: genetic, birth injury, head injury, tumour, stroke, infection (meningitis, neurocysticercosis), febrile, metabolic, alcohol withdrawal.
4. Focal: aware (simple partial), impaired awareness (complex partial), focal to bilateral tonic-clonic.
5. Generalised: tonic-clonic (grand mal), absence (petit mal, 3 Hz spike-wave), myoclonic, atonic, tonic.
6. Status epilepticus: seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated without recovery — emergency.
questions.question: Explain the pathophysiology of epilepsy and classify seizures.

questions.answer:
1. Schizophrenia: positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions), negative (flat affect, withdrawal), cognitive.
2. Dopamine hypothesis: mesolimbic D2 overactivity → positive symptoms; mesocortical underactivity → negative symptoms; amphetamines cause psychosis, antipsychotics block D2. Glutamate (NMDA hypofunction) also involved.
3. Depression: low mood, anhedonia ≥ 2 weeks, sleep and appetite change, guilt, suicidal thoughts.
4. Monoamine hypothesis: reduced noradrenaline and serotonin activity; reserpine causes depression; antidepressants raise monoamines.
5. Delay of weeks in response points to receptor adaptation, HPA axis overactivity (high cortisol) and reduced BDNF.
questions.question: Describe the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia and the monoamine hypothesis of depression.

questions.answer:
1. Stroke: sudden vascular loss of brain function lasting over 24 h; TIA resolves fully.
2. Ischaemic (80–85%): thrombosis on atheroma, cardiac embolism (atrial fibrillation), lacunar disease.
3. Haemorrhagic (15–20%): intracerebral (hypertension), subarachnoid (ruptured berry aneurysm, sudden severe headache).
4. Ischaemic pathophysiology: core infarct with surrounding penumbra; energy failure, glutamate excitotoxicity, Ca2+ influx, free radicals.
5. Risk factors: hypertension (most important), diabetes, smoking, AF, lipids.
6. Features: FAST — face droop, arm weakness, speech difficulty; hemiplegia, sensory and visual loss.
questions.question: Differentiate ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke.

questions.answer: A point mutation in the β-globin gene that replaces glutamic acid by valine at position 6, forming haemoglobin S.
questions.question: What is the mutation in sickle cell anaemia?

questions.answer: B12 is needed for myelin maintenance (methylmalonyl-CoA pathway) as well as DNA synthesis, so its lack causes subacute combined degeneration of the cord; folate is needed only in the DNA pathway.
questions.question: Why does vitamin B12 deficiency cause neurological damage but folate deficiency does not?

questions.answer:
1. Neoplasm: abnormal mass with excessive, uncoordinated growth persisting after the stimulus stops; cancer = malignant neoplasm.
2. Benign vs malignant: slow vs fast growth; capsule vs none; expansion vs invasion; no metastasis vs metastasis; well vs poorly differentiated (anaplasia); uniform vs pleomorphic cells with abnormal mitoses; rare vs common recurrence.
3. Naming: epithelial — papilloma/adenoma vs carcinoma; mesenchymal — lipoma, osteoma vs sarcoma; leukaemia, lymphoma, melanoma.
4. Aetiology: chemicals (tobacco, gutka, aflatoxin, asbestos, benzene), radiation (UV, ionising), viruses (HPV, HBV, HCV, EBV, HTLV-1, HHV-8), H. pylori, hormones, heredity (BRCA, RB, APC), age, obesity, alcohol, chronic inflammation.
5. Pathogenesis: non-lethal DNA damage in one cell → clonal growth.
6. Gene targets: oncogenes activated (RAS, MYC, HER2), tumour suppressors lost (p53, RB, APC — two-hit), apoptosis genes (BCL-2), DNA repair genes.
7. Multistep: initiation → promotion → progression.
8. Hallmarks: growth signals, insensitivity to inhibitors, evasion of apoptosis, limitless replication (telomerase), angiogenesis (VEGF), invasion and metastasis, altered metabolism, immune evasion.
9. Spread: lymphatic (carcinomas), blood (sarcomas; liver, lung, bone), seeding of cavities; grading and TNM staging.
questions.question: What is cancer? Differentiate benign and malignant tumours and describe the aetiology and pathogenesis of cancer.

questions.answer:
1. Jaundice: yellow skin and sclera from raised serum bilirubin; normal below about 1 mg/dL, visible at about 2–3 mg/dL.
2. Metabolism: old RBCs → haem → biliverdin → unconjugated bilirubin (on albumin, not in urine) → liver conjugation by UDP-glucuronyl transferase → conjugated (water-soluble) → bile → gut → urobilinogen → stercobilin (stool) and some urobilinogen in urine.
3. Pre-hepatic (haemolytic): haemolytic anaemias, malaria, transfusion reaction, neonatal; unconjugated bilirubin; no bilirubin in urine; urobilinogen increased; dark stools; normal liver enzymes.
4. Hepatic: viral hepatitis, alcohol, drugs, cirrhosis, Gilbert syndrome; both fractions raised; urine bilirubin present; high ALT/AST.
5. Post-hepatic (obstructive): gallstones, carcinoma head of pancreas, strictures; conjugated raised; dark urine, absent urobilinogen, pale clay stools, itching, high ALP and GGT.
6. Neonatal jaundice and kernicterus risk.
questions.question: Define jaundice. Describe bilirubin metabolism and differentiate pre-hepatic, hepatic and post-hepatic jaundice.

questions.answer:
1. RA: chronic systemic autoimmune disease of synovium; symmetrical polyarthritis; women 3:1.
2. Pathogenesis: HLA-DR4 + trigger (smoking) → citrullinated proteins → autoreactive T and B cells → RF and anti-CCP → TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6 → synovial proliferation = pannus → erosion of cartilage and bone → ankylosis.
3. Features: symmetrical small-joint pain and swelling (MCP, PIP, wrist), morning stiffness > 1 h, ulnar deviation, swan-neck and boutonnière deformities; fatigue, anaemia; nodules, lung fibrosis, vasculitis, Sjögren's.
4. Tests: high ESR/CRP, RF, anti-CCP, X-ray erosions.
5. Gout: hyperuricaemia (saturation about 6.8 mg/dL) → monosodium urate crystals in joints.
6. Causes: under-excretion (90%: CKD, diuretics, low-dose aspirin, pyrazinamide) and over-production (purine-rich food, alcohol, tumour lysis, Lesch–Nyhan).
7. Attack: crystals → neutrophils/macrophages → NLRP3 inflammasome → IL-1β; podagra (first MTP joint).
8. Stages: asymptomatic, acute, intercritical, chronic tophaceous; uric acid stones.
9. Diagnosis: needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals.
questions.question: Describe the pathogenesis, clinical features and complications of rheumatoid arthritis. Add a note on gout.

questions.answer:
1. Site: mouth to anus, terminal ileum vs colon only, starts at rectum.
2. Distribution: skip lesions vs continuous.
3. Depth: transmural vs mucosa and submucosa.
4. Gross: cobblestone, fissures, strictures vs shallow ulcers, pseudopolyps.
5. Microscopy: non-caseating granulomas vs crypt abscesses.
6. Fistulae: common vs rare.
7. Rectal bleeding: less vs common bloody diarrhoea.
8. Smoking: worsens vs protective.
9. Special complications: malabsorption, perianal disease vs toxic megacolon; both raise colon cancer risk.
questions.question: Differentiate Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

questions.answer:
1. A: RNA, faeco-oral, no chronic state, vaccine.
2. B: DNA, blood/sexual/perinatal, chronic in under about 5% of adults but about 90% of infected newborns, cirrhosis and liver cancer, vaccine; HBsAg marker.
3. C: RNA, blood, majority become chronic, cirrhosis and cancer, no vaccine.
4. D: defective virus needing HBsAg of HBV; co-infection or superinfection worsens disease.
5. E: RNA, faeco-oral, water-borne epidemics in India, high mortality in pregnancy.
6. 'F' was proposed but never confirmed as a separate virus.
7. Liver damage mainly from the host T-cell response; outcomes: recovery, fulminant failure, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, carcinoma.
questions.question: Write a comparative note on hepatitis viruses A to E.

questions.answer:
1. Stages: fatty liver (reversible) → alcoholic hepatitis (necrosis, neutrophils, Mallory bodies) → micronodular cirrhosis (irreversible).
2. Acetaldehyde toxicity: binds proteins, damages mitochondria and microtubules.
3. Excess NADH: promotes fat synthesis, blocks fatty acid oxidation.
4. CYP2E1 induction: free radicals, oxidative stress.
5. Endotoxin → Kupffer cells → TNF-α → inflammation.
6. Activated stellate cells → collagen → fibrosis.
7. Complications of cirrhosis: portal hypertension with varices, ascites, encephalopathy, bleeding, jaundice, hormonal changes, hepatorenal syndrome, liver cancer.
questions.question: Describe the stages and pathogenesis of alcoholic liver disease.

questions.answer:
1. Low bone mass with micro-architectural deterioration → fragility and fractures; mineralisation normal.
2. WHO DEXA: T-score −2.5 or lower; osteopenia −1 to −2.5.
3. Mechanism: osteoclastic resorption exceeds osteoblastic formation.
4. Type I postmenopausal: oestrogen loss → more RANKL → trabecular loss → vertebral and wrist fractures.
5. Type II senile: ageing, less calcium and vitamin D → hip fractures.
6. Secondary: corticosteroids, heparin, anticonvulsants, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, Cushing's, immobility.
7. Complications: vertebral collapse, kyphosis, height loss, Colles' and hip fractures.
questions.question: Define osteoporosis and discuss its types, causes and complications.

questions.answer:
1. Proto-oncogenes promote normal growth; gain-of-function mutation, amplification or translocation makes them oncogenes (RAS, MYC, HER2, BCR-ABL) — one mutated copy is enough.
2. Tumour suppressors brake the cell cycle or trigger apoptosis (p53, RB, APC, BRCA); both copies must be lost (Knudson's two-hit).
3. p53 halts the cycle for DNA repair or causes apoptosis — guardian of the genome.
4. Loss of apoptosis genes control (BCL-2 over-expression) lets damaged cells survive.
5. Defective DNA repair speeds mutation.
6. Accumulation of these changes gives uncontrolled growth, invasion and metastasis.
questions.question: Explain how oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes contribute to cancer.

questions.answer: An acute attack of gouty arthritis in the first metatarsophalangeal joint (big toe), the classic first presentation of gout.
questions.question: What is podagra?

questions.answer: Hepatitis A and hepatitis E; both cause acute hepatitis without a chronic state in healthy people.
questions.question: Which hepatitis viruses spread by the faeco-oral route?

questions.answer:
1. Cause: Mycobacterium tuberculosis — slow-growing aerobic acid-fast bacillus (mycolic acid wall; Ziehl–Neelsen stain); M. bovis via milk.
2. Spread: airborne droplet nuclei from open pulmonary TB. Risk: HIV, malnutrition, diabetes, overcrowding, smoking, alcohol, steroids.
3. Pathogenesis: alveolar macrophages ingest bacilli which survive by blocking phagosome–lysosome fusion → Th1 immunity after about 3 weeks → IFN-γ activates macrophages → granuloma of epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, lymphocytes with central caseous necrosis; tuberculin test turns positive.
4. Primary TB: Ghon focus + hilar nodes = Ghon complex; heals with calcification; latent bacilli; may progress (miliary TB, meningitis) in infants and the immunocompromised.
5. Secondary TB: reactivation in apex of upper lobe → caseation → cavity → spread, haemoptysis.
6. Features: cough ≥ 2 weeks, sputum, haemoptysis, chest pain, evening fever, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia.
7. Extrapulmonary: lymph nodes, pleura, spine (Pott's), meninges, abdomen, kidney, bones.
8. Complications: haemoptysis, effusion, empyema, pneumothorax, fibrosis, bronchiectasis, MDR-TB.
9. Diagnosis: sputum AFB smear, CBNAAT/GeneXpert (with rifampicin resistance), culture, chest X-ray, tuberculin test/IGRA, biopsy.
questions.question: Describe the aetiology, pathogenesis, clinical features, complications and diagnosis of tuberculosis.

questions.answer:
1. Cause: HIV-1/HIV-2, RNA retrovirus (lentivirus) with reverse transcriptase.
2. Spread: unprotected sex, blood and products, shared needles, mother to child (pregnancy, delivery, breastfeeding); not by casual contact or insects.
3. Entry: gp120 binds CD4 and co-receptor CCR5 or CXCR4 on helper T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells; gp41 mediates fusion.
4. Replication: reverse transcriptase makes DNA → integrase inserts provirus into host DNA → transcription → protease cleaves proteins → budding.
5. CD4 cell loss by direct killing, immune destruction and apoptosis → loss of cell-mediated immunity.
6. Stages: acute infection (flu-like illness, high viral load), clinical latency (years, lymphadenopathy, falling CD4), symptomatic (weight loss, thrush, zoster), AIDS (CD4 below 200 cells/µL or AIDS-defining illness).
7. Opportunistic infections: tuberculosis (commonest in India), Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, oesophageal candidiasis, cryptococcal meningitis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, CMV retinitis, MAC.
8. Cancers: Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8), non-Hodgkin lymphoma, cervical cancer; HIV dementia, wasting.
9. Diagnosis: ELISA/rapid tests confirmed; CD4 count and viral load for monitoring.
questions.question: Describe the pathogenesis of HIV infection, the stages of the disease and the opportunistic infections of AIDS.

questions.answer:
1. Cause: Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi (paratyphoid A, B, C); gram-negative motile bacillus; humans only host.
2. Spread: faeco-oral via food or water contaminated by patients or carriers; incubation about 10–14 days.
3. Pathogenesis: bacilli invade Peyer's patches via M cells → survive in macrophages → mesenteric nodes → primary bacteraemia → multiply in liver, spleen, marrow → secondary bacteraemia with fever → gallbladder → bile → re-infect intestine → Peyer's patches ulcerate in 2nd–3rd week.
4. Week 1: step-ladder fever, headache, abdominal pain, constipation, relative bradycardia.
5. Week 2: high fever, rose spots, hepatosplenomegaly, coated tongue, toxic state.
6. Week 3: intestinal haemorrhage and perforation, encephalopathy, myocarditis.
7. Other complications: cholecystitis, hepatitis, osteomyelitis, relapse, chronic gallbladder carrier.
8. Diagnosis: blood culture in first week (bone marrow most sensitive); stool and urine culture later; Widal test from second week, rising titre more useful, false positives common.
questions.question: Describe the pathogenesis, clinical features, complications and laboratory diagnosis of typhoid fever.

questions.answer:
1. Cause: Mycobacterium leprae; spread by nasal droplets after prolonged contact; long incubation.
2. Immunity: good cell-mediated (Th1) vs poor (Th2).
3. Bacilli: few vs very many (globi).
4. Lesions: few large well-defined anaesthetic hypopigmented patches vs many symmetrical nodules, leonine facies, loss of eyebrows.
5. Nerves: early asymmetrical thickening vs late symmetrical glove-and-stocking loss.
6. Lepromin test: positive vs negative.
7. Histology: granulomas vs foamy macrophages.
8. Infectivity: low vs high.
9. WHO: paucibacillary (≤5 lesions, smear negative) vs multibacillary (>5 lesions, nerve involvement or smear positive).
questions.question: Differentiate tuberculoid and lepromatous leprosy.

questions.answer:
1. Inflammation of pia and arachnoid.
2. Causes: bacterial (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae b; E. coli, group B strep, Listeria in neonates), viral (enteroviruses), tuberculous, fungal (Cryptococcus in AIDS).
3. Pathogenesis: nasopharyngeal colonisation → bacteraemia → crosses blood–brain barrier → cytokines → neutrophil exudate → raised intracranial pressure.
4. Features: fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, confusion; Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs; purpuric rash in meningococcal disease.
5. CSF bacterial: turbid, neutrophils, high protein, low glucose; viral: clear, lymphocytes, normal glucose; TB: lymphocytes, high protein, low glucose, cobweb.
6. Complications: deafness, hydrocephalus, abscess, seizures, death.
questions.question: Write a note on meningitis with CSF findings.

questions.answer:
1. Cause: Treponema pallidum, spirochaete; spread sexually and across placenta.
2. Primary (about 3 weeks): painless indurated chancre with painless regional lymphadenopathy; heals spontaneously.
3. Secondary (6 weeks–6 months): generalised rash including palms and soles, mucous patches, condylomata lata, fever, lymphadenopathy, patchy alopecia; highly infectious.
4. Latent: no symptoms, serology positive.
5. Tertiary: gummas; cardiovascular (aortitis, aneurysm, aortic regurgitation); neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis, general paresis, Argyll Robertson pupils).
6. Congenital: stillbirth, snuffles, saddle nose, Hutchinson's teeth, sabre shins.
7. Tests: dark-ground microscopy; VDRL/RPR (screening, follow-up); TPHA/FTA-ABS (confirmation).
questions.question: Describe the stages of syphilis.

questions.answer:
1. Infection of bladder (cystitis), urethra, kidney (pyelonephritis) or prostate.
2. Organisms: E. coli (most), Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus, S. saprophyticus, Pseudomonas (catheters).
3. Mostly ascending; fimbriae help adhesion.
4. Risk: female sex, sexual activity, pregnancy, obstruction (prostate, stones), catheters, reflux, diabetes.
5. Cystitis: dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, cloudy urine. Pyelonephritis: fever with rigors, loin pain, vomiting.
6. Diagnosis: dipstick (nitrite, leukocyte esterase), microscopy, culture ≥ 10^5 CFU/ml.
7. Complications: recurrence, renal scarring, abscess, urosepsis, preterm birth.
questions.question: Write a note on urinary tract infection.

questions.answer:
1. Cause: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, gram-negative kidney-shaped intracellular diplococcus; incubation 2–7 days.
2. Pili attach to columnar epithelium of urethra, cervix, rectum, pharynx, conjunctiva → invasion → purulent inflammation; antigenic variation allows reinfection.
3. Men: urethritis, dysuria, thick purulent discharge; epididymitis, prostatitis, stricture.
4. Women: often asymptomatic; cervicitis, discharge; pelvic inflammatory disease → infertility, ectopic pregnancy.
5. Disseminated infection: fever, skin pustules, septic arthritis.
6. Newborn: ophthalmia neonatorum.
7. Diagnosis: Gram stain, culture, NAAT; rising antibiotic resistance.
questions.question: Describe the pathogenesis and clinical features of gonorrhoea.

questions.answer:
1. Airborne/droplet: tuberculosis, meningococcal meningitis.
2. Faeco-oral: typhoid, hepatitis A and E.
3. Sexual contact: HIV, syphilis, gonorrhoea.
4. Blood and needles: hepatitis B and C, HIV.
5. Mother to child: HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B.
6. Insect vectors: malaria, dengue.
7. Prolonged close contact (nasal droplets): leprosy.
8. Ascending from own gut flora: UTI (E. coli).
questions.question: List the routes of transmission of infection with one example each.

questions.answer: The lesion of primary tuberculosis: a small subpleural caseous Ghon focus in the lung plus caseous hilar lymph nodes draining it.
questions.question: What is the Ghon complex?

questions.answer: When the CD4+ T-cell count falls below 200 cells/µL, or an AIDS-defining illness appears, in an HIV-infected person.
questions.question: At what CD4 count is AIDS diagnosed?

# Unit 1: Cell injury, adaptation, inflammation and repair

Pathophysiology explains **why** a disease happens (aetiology), **how** it develops (pathogenesis), and **what** it does to the body (signs, symptoms and complications). This unit builds the base for the whole subject: how a cell keeps its balance, how it adapts to stress, how it gets injured or dies, how the body reacts with inflammation, and how tissue is repaired. It is the longest unit of the syllabus and gives at least one long question in most papers.

## 1.1 Introduction and definitions

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Pathology | Study of disease: structural and functional changes in cells, tissues and organs |
| Pathophysiology | Study of the disturbed physiology (functions) that produce the signs and symptoms of a disease |
| Aetiology | The cause of a disease (bacteria, toxin, gene defect, unknown = idiopathic) |
| Pathogenesis | The sequence of events from the cause to the disease |
| Lesion | The structural change produced in a tissue |
| Sign | What the doctor finds on examination (fever, enlarged liver) |
| Symptom | What the patient feels and reports (pain, nausea) |
| Syndrome | A set of signs and symptoms that occur together |
| Prognosis | The expected outcome of a disease |
| Acute / chronic | Sudden and short-lived / slow and long-lasting |

## 1.2 Homeostasis and feedback systems

**Homeostasis** is the ability of the body to keep its internal environment (temperature, pH, blood glucose, blood pressure, water and electrolytes) nearly constant in spite of changes outside. Disease appears when homeostasis fails.

### Components of a feedback system

```text
Stimulus (change)
      ↓
Receptor (sensor) ── detects the change
      ↓ afferent (input) pathway
Control centre (brain, hypothalamus, endocrine gland) ── compares with set point
      ↓ efferent (output) pathway
Effector (muscle, gland) ── produces a response
      ↓
Response changes the controlled variable  ──► fed back to the receptor
```

### Types of feedback

| Type | What the response does | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Negative feedback | Opposes (reverses) the original change; keeps the variable stable. Most body systems | Body temperature control, baroreceptor control of blood pressure, insulin–glucagon control of blood glucose, thyroid hormone control of TSH |
| Positive feedback | Strengthens the original change until an end event stops it | Oxytocin and uterine contractions in labour, blood clotting cascade, LH surge before ovulation |
| Feed-forward | Body responds before the change happens | Insulin release when food is seen or tasted |

A positive feedback that runs out of control is harmful, e.g. in shock a fall in cardiac output lowers coronary flow, which weakens the heart further.

## 1.3 Cell injury

### Causes of cellular injury

1. **Hypoxia** (oxygen deficiency) — the most common cause. Ischaemia (reduced blood supply), anaemia, CO poisoning, lung disease.
2. **Physical agents** — trauma, extreme heat or cold, radiation, electric shock, sudden pressure change.
3. **Chemical agents and drugs** — poisons (cyanide, arsenic), alcohol, carbon tetrachloride, drug overdose (paracetamol), even high oxygen or salt.
4. **Infectious agents** — viruses, bacteria, fungi, parasites and their toxins.
5. **Immunological reactions** — hypersensitivity, autoimmune disease.
6. **Genetic defects** — sickle cell anaemia, enzyme deficiencies.
7. **Nutritional imbalance** — protein-energy malnutrition, vitamin deficiency, obesity.
8. **Ageing** — reduced ability to repair damage.

### Pathogenesis (mechanisms) of cell injury

The same few biochemical events are seen with most causes.

| Target | What happens | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mitochondria | Hypoxia and toxins stop oxidative phosphorylation; mitochondrial permeability transition pores open; cytochrome c leaks out | ATP depletion, more free radicals, apoptosis |
| Cell membrane | ATP loss stops the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump → Na⁺ and water enter; free radicals cause lipid peroxidation; phospholipases break phospholipids | Cell swelling, loss of permeability, leakage of enzymes |
| Ribosomes | Swelling of rough endoplasmic reticulum and detachment of ribosomes | Protein synthesis falls |
| Nucleus (DNA) | Free radicals, radiation and toxins damage DNA | Apoptosis (if repair fails) or mutation |
| Calcium | Raised cytosolic Ca²⁺ activates phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases and ATPases | Destruction of membranes, proteins and chromatin |
| Free radicals | Superoxide, H2O2, hydroxyl radical from reperfusion, radiation, drugs | Lipid peroxidation, protein cross-links, DNA breaks |

**Sequence in hypoxic (ischaemic) injury**

```text
↓ O2 → ↓ oxidative phosphorylation → ↓ ATP
   ├─ ↓ Na+/K+ pump → Na+ and water enter → cell swelling, ER swelling
   ├─ ↑ anaerobic glycolysis → lactic acid → ↓ pH → chromatin clumping
   └─ ribosomes detach → ↓ protein synthesis
        (all REVERSIBLE if O2 returns)
Continued hypoxia → severe membrane damage + mitochondrial damage + Ca2+ influx
   → lysosomal enzymes leak → NECROSIS (IRREVERSIBLE)
```

Restoring blood flow can sometimes worsen damage (**reperfusion injury**) because fresh oxygen produces a burst of free radicals and brings in calcium and inflammatory cells.

## 1.4 Morphology of cell injury: adaptive changes

When stress is mild or long-lasting, the cell adapts instead of dying.

| Adaptation | Definition | Physiological example | Pathological example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Atrophy | Decrease in the size of cells (and organ) | Thymus after puberty, uterus after menopause | Muscle wasting after nerve injury or plaster, brain atrophy in Alzheimer's, reduced blood supply |
| Hypertrophy | Increase in the size of cells (no new cells) | Skeletal muscle in body builders, uterus in pregnancy | Left ventricular hypertrophy in hypertension and aortic stenosis |
| Hyperplasia | Increase in the number of cells | Breast in puberty and lactation, liver regrowth after partial removal | Endometrial hyperplasia (excess oestrogen), benign prostatic hyperplasia, warts |
| Metaplasia | One adult cell type is replaced by another adult cell type | — | Ciliated columnar → squamous epithelium in smokers' bronchi; squamous → columnar (intestinal type) in lower oesophagus with acid reflux (Barrett's) |
| Dysplasia | Disordered growth: cells vary in size and shape, nuclei large and dark, loss of normal arrangement | — | Cervix, bronchus; a pre-cancerous change that may turn into carcinoma |

Hypertrophy and hyperplasia often occur together (uterus in pregnancy). Hypertrophy alone happens in cells that cannot divide (heart and skeletal muscle). Metaplasia and dysplasia are reversible if the cause is removed, but dysplasia can progress to cancer.

## 1.5 Reversible changes: cell swelling and intracellular accumulation

### Cell swelling (hydropic change)

The first change in almost every injury. Na⁺ and water enter because the pump fails. The cell looks pale and enlarged with small clear vacuoles. The organ becomes heavy and pale. Fully reversible.

### Intracellular accumulations

| Substance | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Lipids (fatty change, steatosis) | Fatty liver in alcoholism, diabetes, obesity, malnutrition, CCl4 poisoning |
| Cholesterol | Foam cells (macrophages full of cholesterol) in atherosclerosis; xanthomas |
| Proteins | Reabsorbed protein droplets in kidney tubules in proteinuria; Russell bodies (immunoglobulin) in plasma cells; Mallory bodies in alcoholic liver |
| Glycogen | Diabetes mellitus, glycogen storage diseases |
| Exogenous pigments | Carbon (anthracosis) in the lungs of city dwellers and coal miners, tattoo ink |
| Endogenous pigments | Lipofuscin ("wear-and-tear" brown pigment of ageing), melanin, haemosiderin (iron overload, old bruise), bilirubin (jaundice) |

## 1.6 Pathological calcification

Abnormal deposition of calcium salts in soft tissues.

| Feature | Dystrophic calcification | Metastatic calcification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tissue | Dead or degenerating tissue | Normal (living) tissue |
| Serum calcium | Normal | Raised (hypercalcaemia) |
| Causes | Atheromas, damaged heart valves, caseous necrosis of TB, dead parasites, fat necrosis | Hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D excess, bone destruction by tumours, chronic renal failure |
| Common sites | Any site of necrosis | Kidneys, lungs, stomach, blood vessels |

## 1.7 Enzyme leakage and cell death

When the membrane of an injured cell is damaged, its enzymes leak into the blood. Measuring them helps diagnosis.

| Enzyme / marker | Organ it points to |
| --- | --- |
| ALT (SGPT), AST (SGOT) | Liver (ALT more specific); AST also heart and muscle |
| Cardiac troponin I or T, CK-MB | Heart muscle (myocardial infarction) |
| Creatine kinase (total) | Skeletal muscle |
| Amylase, lipase | Pancreas |
| Alkaline phosphatase | Bone and bile ducts |
| LDH | Many tissues (non-specific) |

### Necrosis

Death of cells in a living tissue after severe injury, with swelling, membrane rupture and inflammation around it.

| Type | Features | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coagulative | Cell outline kept for some days; proteins denatured | Infarct of heart, kidney (not brain) |
| Liquefactive | Tissue digested into a liquid | Brain infarct, abscess |
| Caseous | Cheese-like, white, crumbly; granuloma around it | Tuberculosis |
| Fat | Fat broken by lipase; calcium soaps form | Acute pancreatitis, breast trauma |
| Fibrinoid | Pink fibrin-like material in vessel wall | Malignant hypertension, vasculitis |
| Gangrene | Necrosis of a large tissue mass; dry (arterial block) or wet (with infection) | Diabetic foot, intestine |

### Apoptosis versus necrosis

| Feature | Apoptosis | Necrosis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | Programmed, controlled ("cell suicide") | Uncontrolled, accidental |
| Cells involved | Single cells | Groups of cells |
| Cell size | Shrinks | Swells |
| Membrane | Intact; forms apoptotic bodies | Ruptured |
| Nucleus | Chromatin condenses, breaks into fragments | Pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis |
| Inflammation | None | Present |
| Enzymes | Caspases | Lysosomal enzymes |
| Examples | Embryo development, removal of old cells, virus-infected cells, DNA damage | Infarction, burns, toxins |

## 1.8 Acidosis and alkalosis

Normal arterial blood: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 35–45 mmHg, HCO3⁻ 22–26 mEq/L. Body defends pH with **buffers** (bicarbonate, phosphate, proteins, haemoglobin), the **lungs** (remove CO2 in minutes) and the **kidneys** (excrete H⁺ and make HCO3⁻ over days).

```text
CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3-
pH = 6.1 + log [HCO3-] / (0.03 × PaCO2)
```

| Disorder | Primary change | Common causes | Compensation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Metabolic acidosis | ↓ HCO3⁻ | Diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis (shock), renal failure, severe diarrhoea, methanol or salicylate poisoning | Hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing) lowers CO2 |
| Metabolic alkalosis | ↑ HCO3⁻ | Prolonged vomiting, nasogastric suction, loop or thiazide diuretics, excess antacid, hypokalaemia | Hypoventilation raises CO2 |
| Respiratory acidosis | ↑ PaCO2 | Hypoventilation: COPD, severe asthma, opioid or sedative overdose, chest wall disease | Kidneys retain HCO3⁻ |
| Respiratory alkalosis | ↓ PaCO2 | Hyperventilation: anxiety, fever, high altitude, early salicylate poisoning, pulmonary embolism | Kidneys excrete HCO3⁻ |

**Anion gap** = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO3⁻), normally about 8–12 mEq/L. It rises in acidosis from added acids (ketones, lactate, renal failure, poisons) and stays normal when bicarbonate is lost (diarrhoea).

Effects: acidosis causes depressed heart contraction, low blood pressure, confusion and hyperkalaemia; alkalosis causes tingling, muscle cramps and tetany (less ionised calcium), arrhythmias and hypokalaemia.

## 1.9 Electrolyte imbalance

| Disorder | Normal range | Causes | Main effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hyponatraemia | Na⁺ 135–145 mEq/L | Excess water (SIADH, heart failure), diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea | Brain swelling: headache, confusion, seizures |
| Hypernatraemia | | Water loss (diabetes insipidus, fever, poor intake) | Thirst, brain shrinkage, confusion, coma |
| Hypokalaemia | K⁺ 3.5–5.0 mEq/L | Diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea, insulin, hyperaldosteronism | Muscle weakness, paralytic ileus, flat T and U waves on ECG, arrhythmias, raised digoxin toxicity |
| Hyperkalaemia | | Renal failure, K⁺-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, acidosis, cell breakdown | Peaked T waves, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest |
| Hypocalcaemia | Total Ca 8.5–10.5 mg/dL | Hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, renal failure | Tetany, carpopedal spasm, seizures, prolonged QT |
| Hypercalcaemia | | Hyperparathyroidism, cancer, vitamin D excess | "Stones, bones, groans and moans": kidney stones, bone pain, constipation, confusion |

## 1.10 Inflammation

**Inflammation** is the protective response of living vascularised tissue to injury. It aims to remove the cause and the dead cells and to start repair. If it is excessive or misdirected it causes disease (asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis).

### Clinical (cardinal) signs

| Sign | Latin | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Redness | Rubor | Vasodilatation, more blood |
| Heat | Calor | Increased blood flow |
| Swelling | Tumor | Exudate leaking from vessels |
| Pain | Dolor | Bradykinin, prostaglandins, pressure on nerves |
| Loss of function | Functio laesa | Pain and swelling (added later by Virchow) |

The first four were described by Celsus.

### Types of inflammation

| Basis | Types |
| --- | --- |
| Duration | Acute (minutes to days; fluid exudate and neutrophils) and chronic (weeks to years; lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells, fibrosis, new vessels) |
| Exudate | Serous (watery: blister, pleural effusion), fibrinous (fibrin-rich: pericarditis), suppurative or purulent (pus: abscess, boil), haemorrhagic, catarrhal (mucus: common cold) |
| Special pattern | Ulcer (loss of surface epithelium: peptic ulcer); granulomatous (collection of epithelioid macrophages and giant cells: tuberculosis, leprosy, sarcoidosis) |

**Acute versus chronic inflammation**

| Feature | Acute | Chronic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Onset | Fast | Slow |
| Main cells | Neutrophils | Macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells |
| Tissue damage | Usually mild, self-limited | Progressive |
| Fibrosis | Little | Marked |
| Examples | Appendicitis, boil, sore throat | Tuberculosis, rheumatoid arthritis, peptic ulcer |

## 1.11 Mechanism of acute inflammation

### A. Vascular events: changes in blood flow and permeability

1. **Brief vasoconstriction** of arterioles (seconds).
2. **Vasodilatation** (histamine, nitric oxide, prostaglandins) → increased flow → redness and heat.
3. **Increased vascular permeability** — protein-rich fluid (exudate) leaks into the tissue → swelling. Mechanisms: contraction of endothelial cells in venules (histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes; quick and short-lived), direct endothelial injury (burns, toxins; prolonged), leukocyte-mediated injury, increased transcytosis (VEGF), and leaky new vessels.
4. **Stasis** — loss of fluid makes blood thick and slow; leukocytes move to the vessel edge.

**Exudate versus transudate**

| Feature | Exudate (inflammation) | Transudate (non-inflammatory, e.g. heart failure) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Protein | High | Low |
| Specific gravity | Above 1.020 | Below 1.012 |
| Cells | Many | Few |
| Cause | Increased permeability | Raised hydrostatic or low oncotic pressure |

### B. Cellular events: migration of white blood cells

```text
Margination → Rolling → Firm adhesion → Transmigration (diapedesis) → Chemotaxis → Phagocytosis
              (selectins)  (integrins on WBC +    (through junctions,        (towards C5a,   (recognition, engulfment,
                           ICAM-1/VCAM-1 on        PECAM-1 / CD31)            LTB4, IL-8,      killing, digestion)
                           endothelium)                                       bacterial products)
```

- **Margination**: slow flow pushes leukocytes to the periphery of the vessel.
- **Rolling**: weak, temporary binding through selectins (E-, P- and L-selectin).
- **Adhesion**: firm binding of leukocyte integrins to endothelial ICAM-1 and VCAM-1, switched on by TNF and IL-1.
- **Transmigration**: cells squeeze between endothelial cells, mainly in venules.
- **Chemotaxis**: movement along a chemical gradient.
- **Phagocytosis**: microbes coated with opsonins (C3b, IgG) are recognised, engulfed into a phagosome, fused with lysosomes and killed by reactive oxygen species (NADPH oxidase, myeloperoxidase forming hypochlorite) and enzymes.

Neutrophils dominate the first 6–24 hours; monocytes/macrophages take over after 24–48 hours.

### C. Mediators of inflammation

| Mediator | Source | Main actions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Histamine | Mast cells, basophils, platelets | Vasodilatation, increased permeability (the earliest mediator) |
| Serotonin (5-HT) | Platelets | Vasodilatation, permeability |
| Prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) | Cyclooxygenase pathway of arachidonic acid | Vasodilatation, pain, fever |
| Thromboxane A2 | Platelets (COX) | Vasoconstriction, platelet aggregation |
| Leukotrienes | Lipoxygenase pathway | LTB4: chemotaxis; LTC4, LTD4, LTE4: bronchoconstriction, permeability |
| Platelet-activating factor | Many cells | Platelet aggregation, bronchoconstriction, permeability |
| Cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) | Macrophages, lymphocytes | Endothelial activation, fever, acute-phase proteins (CRP) |
| Chemokines (IL-8) | Many cells | Chemotaxis |
| Nitric oxide | Endothelium, macrophages | Vasodilatation, microbial killing |
| Complement (C3a, C5a, C3b, C5b–9) | Plasma | C3a/C5a anaphylatoxins (histamine release); C5a chemotaxis; C3b opsonin; membrane attack complex lyses microbes |
| Bradykinin (kinin system) | Plasma | Permeability, vasodilatation, pain |
| Coagulation and fibrinolysis products | Plasma | Thrombin activates endothelium; fibrin split products increase permeability |

```text
Membrane phospholipids
        │ phospholipase A2 (blocked by corticosteroids)
        ▼
  Arachidonic acid
   ├── Cyclooxygenase (blocked by NSAIDs) → PGE2, PGI2, PGF2α, TXA2
   └── 5-Lipoxygenase → LTB4, LTC4, LTD4, LTE4
```

### Systemic effects and outcomes

Fever, raised ESR and CRP, leukocytosis, malaise. Outcomes of acute inflammation: complete resolution, healing by fibrosis (scar), abscess formation, or progression to chronic inflammation.

## 1.12 Basic principles of wound healing in the skin

**Repair** restores tissue by regeneration (same cells grow back — epithelium, liver) and/or by **fibrosis** (connective-tissue scar — where cells cannot divide, or the framework is destroyed).

### Phases of skin wound healing

| Phase | Time (approx.) | Events |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Haemostasis | Minutes | Vasoconstriction, platelet plug, fibrin clot forms a scaffold |
| Inflammation | Days 1–3 | Neutrophils, then macrophages clear debris; growth factors released (PDGF, TGF-β, VEGF, FGF) |
| Proliferation | Days 3–14 | **Granulation tissue** (new capillaries + fibroblasts + loose matrix, pink granular look); epithelium spreads over the surface; collagen (type III first) laid down; myofibroblasts begin contraction |
| Maturation (remodelling) | Weeks to a year or more | Type III collagen replaced by stronger type I; scar becomes pale; strength rises slowly but never fully returns to normal |

### Healing by first and second intention

| Feature | First (primary) intention | Second (secondary) intention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wound | Clean, edges close together (surgical incision with sutures) | Large, gaping, edges apart, infected or with tissue loss (ulcers, burns, abscess) |
| Granulation tissue | Little | Abundant, fills the gap from the base |
| Wound contraction | Minimal | Marked (myofibroblasts) |
| Scar | Thin, neat | Large, may be deforming |
| Time | Fast | Slow |
| Infection risk | Low | High |

### Factors affecting wound healing

- **Local**: infection (the most important), poor blood supply, foreign bodies, movement, large size, radiation, pressure.
- **Systemic**: poor nutrition (protein, vitamin C — needed for collagen hydroxylation, zinc), diabetes mellitus, corticosteroids (suppress inflammation and fibrosis), old age, anaemia, poor circulation, cancer chemotherapy.

Complications: wound infection, wound dehiscence (opening), excess scar (hypertrophic scar, keloid), contractures, incisional hernia.

## 1.13 Pathophysiology of atherosclerosis

**Atherosclerosis** is a chronic inflammatory disease of the intima of large and medium arteries (aorta, coronary, carotid, cerebral, leg arteries) in which lipid-rich plaques (**atheromas**) form, narrow the lumen and may rupture.

### Risk factors

| Non-modifiable | Modifiable |
| --- | --- |
| Increasing age, male sex (women catch up after menopause), family history, genetic lipid disorders | High LDL cholesterol, hypertension, smoking, diabetes mellitus, obesity, physical inactivity, low HDL, raised lipoprotein(a) and homocysteine, chronic inflammation (raised CRP) |

### Pathogenesis: response-to-injury hypothesis

```text
1. Endothelial injury / dysfunction (high BP, smoking, LDL, glucose, toxins)
        ↓  ↑ permeability, ↑ adhesion molecules
2. LDL enters intima → oxidised LDL
        ↓
3. Monocytes adhere, enter, become macrophages
        ↓ take up oxidised LDL via scavenger receptors
4. FOAM CELLS → FATTY STREAK (earliest visible lesion, even in children)
        ↓ cytokines and growth factors (PDGF)
5. Smooth muscle cells migrate from media to intima, multiply, make collagen
        ↓
6. FIBROUS (ATHEROMATOUS) PLAQUE = fibrous cap + lipid/necrotic core
        ↓
7. Complicated plaque: calcification, ulceration, rupture → thrombosis,
   haemorrhage into plaque, embolism, aneurysm
```

### Consequences

- Slow narrowing → reduced blood flow: stable angina, intermittent claudication, chronic ischaemia.
- Plaque rupture + thrombus → sudden block: myocardial infarction, stroke, gangrene of a limb.
- Weakening of the wall → aneurysm, mainly abdominal aorta.

## Remember

- Homeostasis is mostly negative feedback; positive feedback examples: labour (oxytocin), clotting, LH surge.
- ATP depletion, membrane damage, calcium influx and free radicals are the core mechanisms of cell injury.
- Atrophy ↓ size, hypertrophy ↑ size, hyperplasia ↑ number, metaplasia = one adult cell type replaced by another, dysplasia = disordered pre-cancerous growth.
- Dystrophic calcification: dead tissue, normal calcium. Metastatic: normal tissue, high calcium.
- Apoptosis: shrinkage, no inflammation, caspases. Necrosis: swelling, inflammation.
- Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO3⁻); diarrhoea causes normal-gap acidosis, vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis.
- Five signs of inflammation: rubor, calor, tumor, dolor, functio laesa.
- WBC sequence: margination → rolling (selectins) → adhesion (integrins) → transmigration (PECAM-1) → chemotaxis → phagocytosis.
- Steroids block phospholipase A2; NSAIDs block cyclooxygenase.
- Primary intention = clean, close edges, thin scar; secondary = gaping wound, much granulation tissue and contraction.
- Atheroma story: endothelial injury → LDL oxidation → foam cells → fatty streak → fibrous plaque → rupture and thrombosis.
