# Unit 2: Cardiovascular, respiratory and renal diseases

This unit covers the common chronic diseases a pharmacist meets every day at the counter: high blood pressure, heart failure, angina and heart attack, asthma and COPD, and kidney failure. For each disease learn the same five headings: **definition, causes (aetiology), pathogenesis, signs and symptoms, complications**. Hypertension, congestive heart failure, myocardial infarction and asthma are favourite long questions.

## 2.1 Hypertension

**Definition.** A persistent rise of arterial blood pressure. In Indian and most international practice, hypertension is diagnosed when repeated office readings are **140/90 mmHg or above** (some newer guidelines use 130/80 mmHg as the threshold for treatment in high-risk people). Normal is below 120/80 mmHg.

| Category (office BP) | Systolic (mmHg) | Diastolic (mmHg) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal | below 120 | below 80 |
| High normal / prehypertension | 120–139 | 80–89 |
| Stage 1 hypertension | 140–159 | 90–99 |
| Stage 2 hypertension | 160 or more | 100 or more |

### Types

1. **Primary (essential) hypertension** — no single cause; about 90–95% of patients. Genetic tendency plus environment.
2. **Secondary hypertension** — caused by another disease:
   - Renal: chronic kidney disease, renal artery stenosis (renovascular), glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney.
   - Endocrine: primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome), Cushing's syndrome, phaeochromocytoma, hyperthyroidism.
   - Others: coarctation of aorta, pregnancy (pre-eclampsia), drugs (oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, NSAIDs, decongestants), sleep apnoea.

### Pathogenesis

```text
Blood pressure = Cardiac output × Total peripheral resistance
                 (heart rate × stroke volume)   (arteriolar tone)
```

Factors that raise either side cause hypertension:

| Mechanism | How it raises BP |
| --- | --- |
| Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system | Angiotensin II constricts arterioles, releases aldosterone (Na⁺ and water retention), stimulates thirst and sympathetic activity |
| Sympathetic overactivity | Stress → noradrenaline → raised heart rate, contractility and vasoconstriction; renin release |
| Sodium and water retention | High salt intake or kidney defect → larger blood volume |
| Endothelial dysfunction | Less nitric oxide, more endothelin → vasoconstriction |
| Structural change | Vessel walls thicken (remodelling), so resistance stays high |
| Others | Obesity, insulin resistance, genetics, ageing (stiff arteries raise systolic BP) |

```text
↓ renal perfusion → kidney releases RENIN
Angiotensinogen (liver) --renin--> Angiotensin I --ACE (lungs)--> Angiotensin II
Angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone (Na+/H2O retention) + ADH + thirst
            → ↑ peripheral resistance + ↑ blood volume → ↑ BP
```

### Signs and symptoms

Usually **none** — the "silent killer" — found on routine check. Some patients have morning headache at the back of the head, dizziness, palpitations, nosebleed, blurred vision.

### Complications (target-organ damage)

| Organ | Damage |
| --- | --- |
| Heart | Left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction |
| Brain | Stroke (haemorrhage and infarct), hypertensive encephalopathy, dementia |
| Kidney | Nephrosclerosis, chronic kidney disease |
| Eyes | Hypertensive retinopathy (narrowed arteries, haemorrhages, papilloedema) |
| Vessels | Accelerated atherosclerosis, aortic dissection, aneurysm, peripheral arterial disease |

**Hypertensive crisis**: a very high reading (often around 180/120 mmHg or more). If organ damage is present (encephalopathy, pulmonary oedema, MI) it is an emergency.

## 2.2 Congestive heart failure

**Definition.** The heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the needs of the tissues, or can do so only at raised filling pressures. "Congestive" because blood backs up in the lungs and/or the veins of the body.

### Causes

- Ischaemic heart disease (most common), myocardial infarction.
- Hypertension (pressure overload).
- Valve disease (aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation), cardiomyopathy, myocarditis.
- Arrhythmias, congenital heart disease.
- High-output states: severe anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, beriberi.
- Precipitating factors: infection, uncontrolled BP, non-adherence, excess salt or fluid, NSAIDs.

### Types

| Basis | Types |
| --- | --- |
| Function | Systolic failure (weak contraction, reduced ejection fraction) and diastolic failure (stiff ventricle, poor filling, ejection fraction preserved) |
| Side | Left-sided and right-sided (most patients end up with both) |
| Speed | Acute (e.g. after MI) and chronic |
| Output | Low-output (most) and high-output (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis) |

### Pathogenesis: compensation that becomes harmful

```text
Damaged heart → ↓ cardiac output → ↓ BP and renal perfusion
   ├─ Sympathetic activation → ↑ HR, contractility, vasoconstriction (more workload)
   ├─ RAAS activation → Na+/water retention, vasoconstriction (more preload + afterload)
   ├─ ADH release → water retention
   ├─ Frank–Starling: more filling → stronger beat (only up to a point)
   └─ Ventricular remodelling/hypertrophy → stiff, enlarged, failing heart
These keep output up at first, but in the long run they overload the heart
and the cycle worsens → oedema, congestion.
```

### Signs and symptoms

| Left heart failure (lung congestion) | Right heart failure (systemic congestion) |
| --- | --- |
| Breathlessness on exertion (dyspnoea), orthopnoea (breathless lying flat), paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea | Swelling of ankles and legs (pitting oedema) |
| Cough, frothy pink sputum in acute pulmonary oedema | Raised jugular venous pressure |
| Fine crackles at lung bases, third heart sound | Enlarged tender liver, ascites |
| Fatigue, cold peripheries | Loss of appetite, nausea (gut congestion) |

Most common cause of right heart failure is left heart failure. Right failure due to lung disease is called **cor pulmonale**.

**NYHA functional classes**: I no limitation; II slight limitation, symptoms on ordinary activity; III marked limitation, symptoms on less than ordinary activity; IV symptoms at rest.

**Complications**: pulmonary oedema, arrhythmias, sudden death, kidney failure, thromboembolism, liver congestion (cardiac cirrhosis), cachexia.

## 2.3 Ischaemic heart disease

**Definition.** A group of conditions caused by an imbalance between the oxygen supply of the heart muscle (coronary blood flow) and its oxygen demand. More than 90% of cases are due to **atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries** (coronary artery disease).

```text
Supply ↓ : atherosclerotic narrowing, thrombosis, spasm, anaemia, hypotension
Demand ↑ : exercise, tachycardia, hypertension, LVH, emotion, cold
               ↓
          MYOCARDIAL ISCHAEMIA
   ┌───────────┼───────────┬────────────┐
 Angina     Acute MI    Chronic IHD   Sudden cardiac death
```

### Angina pectoris

Chest pain from transient ischaemia **without** muscle death. Typically a squeezing or heavy pain behind the sternum, spreading to the left arm, neck or jaw, lasting a few minutes.

| Type | Mechanism | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stable (classic, exertional) | Fixed atherosclerotic narrowing; demand exceeds supply | Comes on exercise, emotion or cold; relieved by rest or sublingual nitrate in minutes |
| Unstable (crescendo) | Plaque rupture with a non-occlusive thrombus | Pain at rest, more frequent or longer; high risk of MI. Part of acute coronary syndrome |
| Variant (Prinzmetal) | Coronary artery spasm | Pain at rest, often early morning; ST elevation during the attack; relieved by nitrates and calcium channel blockers |

### Myocardial infarction (heart attack)

**Death (necrosis) of heart muscle** due to prolonged ischaemia, usually from a thrombus on a ruptured coronary plaque.

**Pathogenesis**

```text
Unstable plaque ruptures → platelets adhere and aggregate (TXA2, ADP)
→ coagulation → occlusive thrombus → no flow
→ ATP depletion within seconds, loss of contraction within about a minute
→ irreversible injury after roughly 20–40 minutes of severe ischaemia
→ necrosis spreads from subendocardium to the whole wall over a few hours
```

Hence "time is muscle" — opening the artery early (thrombolysis or angioplasty) saves myocardium.

**Types**: transmural (full-thickness, usually STEMI) and subendocardial (inner layer, usually NSTEMI).

**Clinical features**: severe crushing chest pain over 20–30 minutes, not relieved by rest or nitrates; sweating, nausea, vomiting, breathlessness, anxiety, sense of impending death. Elderly and diabetic patients may have a "silent" MI with little pain.

**Diagnosis**
- **ECG**: ST-segment elevation (STEMI) or ST depression/T inversion (NSTEMI); pathological Q waves later.
- **Cardiac markers**: troponin I or T (most specific; rises within a few hours and stays high for 1–2 weeks), CK-MB, myoglobin (early but non-specific).

**Complications**: arrhythmias (ventricular fibrillation — main cause of early death), heart failure and cardiogenic shock, rupture of wall, septum or papillary muscle, ventricular aneurysm, pericarditis, mural thrombus with embolism, recurrent infarction.

### Atherosclerosis and arteriosclerosis

**Arteriosclerosis** means "hardening of the arteries" — thickening and loss of elasticity of the arterial wall. It has three forms:

| Form | Vessels | Feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Atherosclerosis | Large and medium arteries | Lipid-rich intimal plaques (atheromas); the most important form (pathogenesis in Unit 1) |
| Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis | Medium muscular arteries, elderly | Calcium in the media; lumen not narrowed |
| Arteriolosclerosis | Small arteries and arterioles | Hyaline (hypertension, diabetes, ageing) or hyperplastic "onion-skin" (malignant hypertension) |

So every atherosclerosis is arteriosclerosis, but not every arteriosclerosis is atherosclerosis.

## 2.4 Bronchial asthma

**Definition.** A chronic inflammatory disease of the airways with **reversible** (variable) airflow obstruction, bronchial hyper-responsiveness and recurrent wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough, worse at night and early morning.

### Types

| Type | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Extrinsic (allergic, atopic) | Starts in childhood; triggered by allergens (pollen, house-dust mite, animal dander, moulds); raised IgE; family history of eczema, hay fever |
| Intrinsic (non-allergic) | Starts in adults; triggers are infection, cold air, exercise, stress, pollution; IgE not raised |
| Drug-induced | Aspirin and NSAIDs (shift arachidonic acid to leukotrienes), β-blockers |
| Occupational | Isocyanates, flour, wood dust |
| Exercise-induced | Cooling and drying of airways |

### Pathogenesis (allergic asthma)

```text
Sensitisation: allergen → dendritic cells → Th2 cells → IL-4, IL-5, IL-13
               → B cells make IgE → IgE binds to mast cells
Re-exposure:
 EARLY PHASE (minutes): allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells
   → histamine, leukotrienes C4/D4/E4, prostaglandin D2, PAF
   → bronchospasm, mucosal oedema, mucus secretion
 LATE PHASE (4–8 h): eosinophils, Th2 cells, neutrophils arrive
   → more inflammation, epithelial damage, hyper-responsiveness
Chronic: AIRWAY REMODELLING – thick basement membrane, smooth-muscle
   hypertrophy, goblet-cell hyperplasia, mucus plugs
```

**Signs and symptoms**: episodic wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness, dry cough (especially at night); prolonged expiration; reduced peak expiratory flow which improves after a bronchodilator.

**Complications**: status asthmaticus (severe attack not responding to usual treatment — an emergency), respiratory failure, pneumothorax, chest infections, side effects of long-term treatment.

## 2.5 Chronic obstructive airways disease (COPD)

**Definition.** A common, preventable disease with **persistent, poorly reversible** airflow limitation that usually progresses, caused by a long-term inflammatory response of the lungs to noxious particles or gases — mainly **cigarette smoking**, and in India also biomass (wood, dung) smoke from household cooking. Spirometry: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70.

It includes two overlapping conditions:

| Feature | Chronic bronchitis ("blue bloater") | Emphysema ("pink puffer") |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definition | Productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years | Permanent enlargement of airspaces beyond the terminal bronchiole with destruction of alveolar walls, without obvious fibrosis |
| Main lesion | Mucus gland hypertrophy, goblet-cell hyperplasia, inflamed narrow airways | Loss of alveolar walls and elastic recoil; airways collapse on expiration |
| Mechanism | Irritants → mucus hypersecretion → infection | Protease–antiprotease imbalance: smoke attracts neutrophils and macrophages releasing elastase, and oxidants inactivate α1-antitrypsin; inherited α1-antitrypsin deficiency gives panacinar emphysema |
| Picture | Cough with sputum, cyanosis, oedema, early cor pulmonale | Marked breathlessness, pursed-lip breathing, barrel chest, thin patient |
| Gases | Low O2, high CO2 early | O2 fairly kept until late |

Smoking gives **centriacinar** (centrilobular) emphysema of upper lobes; α1-antitrypsin deficiency gives **panacinar** emphysema of lower lobes.

**Complications**: acute exacerbations (often infection), respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, secondary polycythaemia, pneumothorax from ruptured bullae, lung cancer (shared smoking risk).

**Asthma vs COPD**: asthma — younger, allergic, reversible, eosinophils; COPD — older smokers, little reversibility, neutrophils, progressive.

## 2.6 Acute renal failure (acute kidney injury)

**Definition.** A sudden fall (hours to days) in kidney function, with rising serum creatinine and urea and often reduced urine output (**oliguria** = less than 400 ml/day; **anuria** = less than about 100 ml/day). It is often reversible.

### Causes

| Group | Mechanism | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-renal (most common) | Kidney normal but under-perfused | Dehydration (vomiting, diarrhoea, burns), haemorrhage, shock, heart failure, NSAIDs or ACE inhibitors in a dry patient |
| Renal (intrinsic) | Damage to kidney tissue | Acute tubular necrosis (prolonged ischaemia; nephrotoxic drugs such as aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, contrast media; myoglobin, haemoglobin), acute glomerulonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis (drug allergy) |
| Post-renal | Block to urine outflow | Stones, enlarged prostate, tumours, blocked catheter |

### Pathogenesis of acute tubular necrosis

Ischaemia or toxins damage tubular cells → cells shed into the lumen and form casts that block tubules → filtrate leaks back through damaged walls → GFR falls; reflex vasoconstriction (via tubuloglomerular feedback) lowers GFR further.

### Phases

1. **Initiation** — the insult; output starts to fall.
2. **Oliguric (maintenance)** — low urine output; urea, creatinine, K⁺ and H⁺ rise; fluid overload.
3. **Diuretic (recovery) phase** — tubules heal but cannot yet concentrate urine → large urine volume; risk of dehydration, low K⁺ and Na⁺.
4. **Recovery** — function returns to normal over weeks.

**Effects**: fluid overload (oedema, pulmonary oedema, hypertension), hyperkalaemia (arrhythmias), metabolic acidosis, uraemia (nausea, confusion, pericarditis), drug accumulation — doses of renally excreted drugs must be reduced.

## 2.7 Chronic renal failure (chronic kidney disease)

**Definition.** Kidney damage or reduced function (GFR below 60 ml/min/1.73 m²) lasting **more than 3 months**; slowly progressive and irreversible. End-stage renal disease (GFR below 15) needs dialysis or a transplant.

| Stage | GFR (ml/min/1.73 m²) |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 90 or more, with kidney damage |
| 2 | 60–89 |
| 3a / 3b | 45–59 / 30–44 |
| 4 | 15–29 |
| 5 (kidney failure) | below 15 |

**Causes**: diabetic nephropathy (most common), hypertension, chronic glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney disease, chronic pyelonephritis and obstruction, long-term analgesic or other nephrotoxic drug use.

**Pathogenesis**: nephrons are lost; the remaining nephrons hyperfilter to compensate → raised glomerular pressure → further glomerular sclerosis and loss of more nephrons (a vicious cycle). Proteinuria and angiotensin II speed the damage.

### Clinical features and complications

| System | Problem and cause |
| --- | --- |
| Fluid / electrolytes | Oedema, hypertension, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, hyponatraemia |
| Blood | Normocytic anaemia — lack of **erythropoietin**; bleeding tendency |
| Bone | **Renal osteodystrophy** — less activation of vitamin D (1-α hydroxylation), phosphate retention, hypocalcaemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism |
| Uraemia | Nausea, vomiting, itching, metallic taste, confusion, pericarditis, neuropathy, uraemic breath |
| Heart | Hypertension, LVH, heart failure, accelerated atherosclerosis — the main cause of death |
| Urine | Early nocturia and polyuria (cannot concentrate); later oliguria |

**Acute vs chronic**: acute — sudden, often reversible, kidneys normal size; chronic — slow, irreversible, kidneys usually small and scarred, with anaemia and bone disease.

## Remember

- BP = cardiac output × peripheral resistance; RAAS and sympathetic system are central in hypertension. Essential hypertension ≈ 90–95%.
- Hypertension damages heart, brain, kidney, eyes and vessels; usually no symptoms.
- Heart failure compensations (SNS, RAAS, ADH, remodelling) help at first, then worsen failure. Left failure → lungs; right failure → legs, liver, neck veins.
- Stable angina: exertion, relieved by rest; unstable: at rest, plaque rupture; Prinzmetal: spasm.
- MI = necrosis; troponin is the most specific marker; ventricular fibrillation causes most early deaths.
- Arteriosclerosis is the umbrella term; atherosclerosis is its lipid-plaque form.
- Asthma: Th2, IgE, mast cells, early and late phases, reversible. COPD: smoking, neutrophils, protease–antiprotease, poorly reversible.
- AKI: pre-renal, renal (ATN), post-renal; oliguria < 400 ml/day; watch hyperkalaemia.
- CKD: GFR < 60 for > 3 months; anaemia (EPO), renal osteodystrophy (vitamin D), uraemia; diabetes is the top cause.

# Unit 3: Blood, endocrine, nervous system disorders and peptic ulcer

This unit covers four systems: anaemias and haemophilia, diabetes and thyroid and sex-hormone disorders, the major brain disorders (epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, stroke, depression, schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease) and peptic ulcer. It is a large unit, so it usually supplies one long question and two or three short ones. Diabetes mellitus, anaemias, Parkinson's disease and peptic ulcer appear most often.

## 3.1 Anaemia: general points

**Anaemia** is a fall in the haemoglobin concentration (or red cell mass) below normal for age and sex, so that the blood carries less oxygen. WHO cut-offs: below **13 g/dL in adult men**, below **12 g/dL in non-pregnant women**, below **11 g/dL in pregnancy**.

**Common symptoms**: tiredness, weakness, breathlessness on exertion, palpitations, dizziness, headache, pallor of skin, nails and conjunctiva; in severe cases angina and heart failure.

**Classification by red cell size (MCV)**

| Type | MCV | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Microcytic hypochromic | Low (small, pale cells) | Iron deficiency, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease (some) |
| Normocytic normochromic | Normal | Acute blood loss, chronic kidney disease, aplastic anaemia, haemolytic anaemias |
| Macrocytic | High (large cells) | Vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency (megaloblastic), alcohol, liver disease |

**Classification by cause**: blood loss; reduced production (deficiency of iron, B12, folate; marrow failure); increased destruction (haemolytic anaemias: sickle cell, thalassaemia, G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis, autoimmune).

## 3.2 Iron deficiency anaemia

The most common anaemia in the world and in India, especially in women and children.

**Causes**
- Chronic blood loss — the main cause in adults: heavy menstruation, peptic ulcer, piles, hookworm infestation, gut cancer, regular NSAID use.
- Increased need — pregnancy, lactation, growing children.
- Poor intake — vegetarian diet low in iron, poverty.
- Poor absorption — achlorhydria, gastrectomy, coeliac disease (iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum, in the ferrous form).

**Pathogenesis**: body iron stores (ferritin) are used up first → serum iron falls and transferrin (TIBC) rises → haem synthesis fails → small, pale red cells.

**Features**: general anaemia symptoms plus spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), brittle nails, smooth tongue (glossitis), cracks at mouth corners (angular stomatitis), craving for non-food items such as clay or ice (pica), difficulty swallowing from oesophageal webs.

**Blood findings**: low Hb, low MCV and MCH, microcytic hypochromic cells, **low serum ferritin** (best single test), low serum iron, high TIBC.

## 3.3 Megaloblastic anaemia (vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency)

Both vitamins are needed for **DNA synthesis** (thymidine production). When either is lacking, the nucleus matures more slowly than the cytoplasm, so the marrow makes large abnormal precursors (**megaloblasts**) and large red cells (macrocytes). Many die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis).

| Feature | Vitamin B12 deficiency | Folic acid deficiency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sources | Animal foods only (meat, fish, eggs, milk) | Green leafy vegetables, liver, legumes; destroyed by long cooking |
| Body stores | Large (lasts a few years) | Small (lasts a few months) |
| Main causes | **Pernicious anaemia** (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells), strict vegetarian diet, gastrectomy, ileal disease or resection, fish tapeworm | Poor diet, pregnancy, alcoholism, malabsorption, haemolysis, drugs (methotrexate, phenytoin, trimethoprim) |
| Neurological signs | **Yes** — subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, numbness and tingling, loss of vibration and position sense, memory loss | No |
| Special point | Giving folic acid alone may correct the blood picture but let nerve damage progress | Deficiency in early pregnancy raises the risk of neural tube defects |

**Blood picture**: raised MCV, oval macrocytes, **hypersegmented neutrophils** (5 or more lobes), low reticulocytes, raised LDH and bilirubin (destruction in marrow). Glossitis (red beefy tongue) and mild jaundice are common.

## 3.4 Sickle cell anaemia

An **inherited (autosomal recessive)** disorder caused by a point mutation in the β-globin gene: glutamic acid at position 6 is replaced by **valine**, producing **haemoglobin S**.

```text
Low O2 / dehydration / acidosis / infection
→ HbS polymerises into long rigid fibres
→ red cell becomes sickle-shaped and stiff
→ (1) cells block small vessels → ISCHAEMIA, pain crises, infarcts
→ (2) cells destroyed early → HAEMOLYTIC ANAEMIA
```

- Homozygous (HbSS) = sickle cell disease; heterozygous (HbAS) = sickle cell trait, usually symptom-free, and partly protected against falciparum malaria.
- **Features**: chronic haemolytic anaemia with jaundice and gallstones; painful (vaso-occlusive) crises in bones, chest and abdomen; hand–foot swelling in infants; stroke; acute chest syndrome; leg ulcers; priapism; **autosplenectomy** (spleen destroyed by repeated infarcts) → serious infections (pneumococcus, Salmonella osteomyelitis); aplastic crisis with parvovirus B19.
- In India it is common in tribal populations of central, western and southern states.

## 3.5 Thalassaemia

Inherited (autosomal recessive) disorders in which **too little** of one globin chain is made, although the chain itself is normal. The excess unpaired chain precipitates in red cells and their precursors, causing ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis.

| Type | Defect | Forms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| β-thalassaemia | Reduced (β+) or absent (β0) β-chain synthesis, mostly point mutations | **Major** (Cooley's anaemia, homozygous): severe anaemia from about 6 months of age, needs regular transfusion; **minor/trait** (heterozygous): mild microcytosis, no symptoms; intermedia: between the two |
| α-thalassaemia | Deletion of α-globin genes (4 genes normally) | Silent carrier (1 deleted), trait (2), HbH disease (3), hydrops fetalis (all 4, fatal before birth) |

**Features of thalassaemia major**: severe anaemia, failure to thrive, enlarged liver and spleen, marrow expansion causing "chipmunk" face and "hair-on-end" skull X-ray, and **iron overload** from transfusions and increased absorption (heart failure, liver cirrhosis, diabetes, delayed puberty) — hence iron chelation. Blood: microcytic hypochromic cells, target cells, raised HbF and HbA2 (on electrophoresis in β-thalassaemia).

## 3.6 Hereditary and acquired anaemias

The syllabus groups anaemias by origin.

| Hereditary (inherited) | Acquired |
| --- | --- |
| Sickle cell anaemia, thalassaemias (haemoglobin defects) | Nutritional: iron, B12, folate deficiency |
| Hereditary spherocytosis (red cell membrane defect; spherical fragile cells removed by the spleen) | Blood loss: acute or chronic |
| G6PD deficiency (enzyme defect, X-linked; haemolysis after oxidant drugs such as primaquine, sulfonamides, dapsone, or fava beans, infection) | Aplastic anaemia (marrow failure from drugs such as chloramphenicol, radiation, viruses, autoimmune) |
| Fanconi anaemia (inherited marrow failure) | Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia; drug-induced haemolysis; malaria |
| | Anaemia of chronic disease (infection, inflammation, cancer), anaemia of kidney disease (low erythropoietin) |

## 3.7 Haemophilia

An inherited **bleeding disorder** due to deficiency of a clotting factor.

| Feature | Haemophilia A | Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deficient factor | Factor VIII | Factor IX |
| Frequency | More common (about 80–85%) | Less common |
| Inheritance | X-linked recessive | X-linked recessive |

- Males are affected; females are usually carriers; there is no male-to-male transmission.
- **Features**: easy bruising, prolonged bleeding after cuts, tooth extraction or surgery; deep bleeding into **joints (haemarthrosis)** — knees, elbows, ankles — leading to crippling arthritis; bleeding into muscles; bleeding in the brain can be fatal. Severity depends on the factor level.
- **Tests**: prolonged aPTT; normal PT, platelet count and bleeding time; low factor assay.
- Avoid aspirin, NSAIDs and intramuscular injections.

## 3.8 Diabetes mellitus

**Definition.** A group of metabolic disorders with chronic **hyperglycaemia** due to a defect in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both, with disturbed carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism.

**Diagnostic criteria** (any one, confirmed on repeat if no symptoms):
- Fasting plasma glucose **126 mg/dL or more** (normal below 100).
- 2-hour plasma glucose **200 mg/dL or more** in a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test.
- HbA1c **6.5% or more**.
- Random plasma glucose 200 mg/dL or more with classic symptoms.

### Types

| Feature | Type 1 | Type 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cause | Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells (T cells; antibodies to GAD, islet cells, insulin) in a genetically prone person, often after a viral trigger | Insulin resistance in muscle, fat and liver + progressive β-cell dysfunction |
| Insulin level | Absent or very low | Normal, high or relatively low |
| Age of onset | Usually children and young adults | Usually adults over 30–40 (now younger, with obesity) |
| Body build | Usually thin | Usually overweight, central obesity |
| Onset | Sudden | Slow; often found by chance |
| Ketoacidosis | Common | Rare |
| Share of cases | About 5–10% | About 90% |
| Treatment | Insulin essential | Diet, exercise, oral drugs; insulin later if needed |

Other types: **gestational diabetes** (first detected in pregnancy), and secondary diabetes (pancreatitis, Cushing's syndrome, corticosteroid therapy, acromegaly).

### Pathophysiology of the symptoms

```text
↓ insulin action
├─ ↓ glucose uptake by muscle/fat + ↑ liver glucose output → HYPERGLYCAEMIA
│     → glucose in urine (above renal threshold ≈ 180 mg/dL) → osmotic diuresis
│     → POLYURIA → dehydration → POLYDIPSIA (thirst)
├─ cells "starve" → POLYPHAGIA, weight loss, fatigue
├─ ↑ fat breakdown → free fatty acids → liver makes KETONE bodies → ketoacidosis
└─ ↑ protein breakdown → muscle wasting, poor healing
```

### Complications

| Acute | Chronic: microvascular | Chronic: macrovascular | Others |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Diabetic ketoacidosis (mainly type 1): hyperglycaemia, ketosis, metabolic acidosis, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath, dehydration | Retinopathy (leading cause of blindness) | Coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction | Infections (skin, urinary, TB, fungal) |
| Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (mainly type 2): very high glucose, severe dehydration, little ketosis | Nephropathy (proteinuria → chronic kidney disease) | Stroke | Diabetic foot: neuropathy + poor circulation + infection → ulcer, gangrene, amputation |
| Hypoglycaemia (from insulin or sulfonylureas): sweating, tremor, confusion, coma | Neuropathy (glove-and-stocking numbness, autonomic neuropathy) | Peripheral arterial disease | Cataract |

Long-term high glucose damages tissue by glycation of proteins (advanced glycation end products), the polyol (sorbitol) pathway and oxidative stress.

## 3.9 Thyroid diseases

Thyroid hormones (T4 and T3) control the metabolic rate. Release is controlled by **TRH** (hypothalamus) → **TSH** (pituitary) → thyroid, with negative feedback. Iodine is needed for hormone synthesis.

### Hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis)

**Causes**: **Graves' disease** (most common; autoimmune — antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor), toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis, excess thyroid hormone tablets or iodine.

**Features**: weight loss with good appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, tremor, anxiety, irritability, diarrhoea, menstrual disturbance, goitre. Graves' disease adds **exophthalmos** (bulging eyes) and pretibial myxoedema. Blood: high T3/T4, low TSH. Severe form: thyroid storm.

### Hypothyroidism

**Causes**: **Hashimoto's thyroiditis** (autoimmune destruction, the most common in iodine-sufficient areas), iodine deficiency (still seen in hilly regions of India), after surgery or radioiodine, drugs (lithium, amiodarone), pituitary disease.

**Features**: tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry coarse skin, hair loss, hoarse voice, constipation, slow pulse, puffy face, heavy periods, depression, slow reflexes. Severe adult form = **myxoedema** (non-pitting swelling; myxoedema coma). In infants = **cretinism**: mental retardation, short stature, coarse face, large tongue, umbilical hernia — hence newborn screening. Blood: low T4, high TSH (primary).

### Goitre

Enlargement of the thyroid. May be simple (iodine deficiency), multinodular, toxic or non-toxic. Low hormone → high TSH → gland enlarges.

## 3.10 Disorders of sex hormones

| Disorder | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Male hypogonadism | Low testosterone. Primary (testis failure: Klinefelter syndrome 47,XXY, mumps orchitis, injury) or secondary (pituitary/hypothalamus failure). Features: reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, infertility, less body hair, gynaecomastia |
| Female hypogonadism | Ovarian failure (Turner syndrome 45,XO, premature ovarian failure) or pituitary causes; amenorrhoea, infertility, osteoporosis |
| Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) | Common; excess androgens, irregular or absent ovulation, multiple small ovarian cysts; acne, hirsutism, obesity, infertility, insulin resistance |
| Hirsutism | Male-pattern hair growth in women due to excess androgens |
| Gynaecomastia | Breast enlargement in men from a high oestrogen-to-androgen ratio (puberty, liver cirrhosis, drugs such as spironolactone) |
| Menopause | Natural fall in oestrogen: hot flushes, mood change, vaginal dryness, osteoporosis, raised cardiovascular risk |
| Precocious / delayed puberty | Puberty too early or too late |
| Hyperprolactinaemia | Pituitary tumour or drugs (antipsychotics): galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, infertility |

## 3.11 Epilepsy

**Seizure**: a sudden, abnormal, excessive and synchronised electrical discharge of brain neurons causing altered movement, sensation, behaviour or consciousness. **Epilepsy**: a tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures (two or more).

**Pathophysiology**: imbalance between excitation (glutamate, Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ channels) and inhibition (GABA). Causes include genetic factors, head injury, birth injury, brain tumours, stroke, infections (meningitis, neurocysticercosis — common in India), fever in children, alcohol withdrawal, metabolic upsets (low glucose, low Na⁺).

| Class | Type | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Focal (partial) | Focal aware (simple partial) | Twitching of one limb or odd sensation; consciousness kept |
| | Focal impaired awareness (complex partial) | Altered awareness, automatisms (lip smacking); often temporal lobe |
| | Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic | Starts focal, spreads to both sides |
| Generalised | Tonic-clonic (grand mal) | Loss of consciousness, stiffening (tonic) then jerking (clonic), tongue bite, incontinence, confusion afterwards |
| | Absence (petit mal) | Children; brief blank spells of a few seconds; 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG |
| | Myoclonic, atonic, tonic | Sudden jerks; sudden loss of tone (drop attacks) |

**Status epilepticus**: continuous seizure activity, or repeated seizures without recovery between them, lasting 5 minutes or more — an emergency.

## 3.12 Parkinson's disease

A progressive degenerative movement disorder of older people.

**Pathogenesis**: loss of **dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra (pars compacta)** that project to the striatum (nigrostriatal pathway). Surviving neurons contain **Lewy bodies** (aggregates of α-synuclein). Low dopamine with relatively high acetylcholine in the striatum disturbs the basal ganglia circuits. Symptoms appear only after a large part of these neurons has been lost. Possible causes: ageing, genes, environmental toxins (MPTP, pesticides), oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction.

**Features (TRAP)**
- **T**remor at rest ("pill-rolling"), lessened by movement.
- **R**igidity ("lead-pipe" or "cog-wheel").
- **A**kinesia / bradykinesia (slow, little movement): mask-like face, small handwriting, reduced blinking.
- **P**ostural instability: stooped posture, shuffling festinating gait, falls.
- Non-motor: depression, constipation, sleep problems, loss of smell, dementia later.

**Secondary parkinsonism**: antipsychotics (dopamine D2 blockers), metoclopramide, head injury, repeated stroke.

## 3.13 Stroke

**Definition.** Sudden loss of brain function lasting more than 24 hours (or leading to death) due to a vascular cause. **Transient ischaemic attack (TIA)**: same symptoms that resolve fully, usually within an hour — a warning sign.

| Type | About | Causes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ischaemic (infarction) | 80–85% | Thrombosis on an atherosclerotic plaque (carotid, cerebral arteries), embolism from the heart (atrial fibrillation, after MI), small-vessel (lacunar) disease |
| Haemorrhagic | 15–20% | Intracerebral haemorrhage (hypertension), subarachnoid haemorrhage (ruptured berry aneurysm, sudden "worst-ever" headache) |

**Pathophysiology of ischaemic stroke**: blocked flow → central core dies within minutes; around it lies the **penumbra**, which can be saved if flow returns quickly. Energy failure → glutamate release → Ca²⁺ influx (excitotoxicity) → free radicals and inflammation → cell death.

**Risk factors**: hypertension (the most important), diabetes, smoking, atrial fibrillation, high cholesterol, obesity, alcohol, age.

**Features (FAST)**: **F**ace drooping, **A**rm weakness, **S**peech difficulty, **T**ime to call for help. Also one-sided paralysis (hemiplegia), sensory loss, vision loss, imbalance, coma.

## 3.14 Psychiatric disorders

### Depression (major depressive disorder)

**Features** (most days for **at least 2 weeks**): low mood, loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia), poor or increased sleep and appetite, fatigue, poor concentration, guilt or worthlessness, slowed movement or agitation, thoughts of death or suicide.

**Pathophysiology**
- **Monoamine hypothesis**: reduced activity of noradrenaline and serotonin (5-HT), and dopamine, in the brain. Supported by reserpine (depletes monoamines) causing depression and antidepressants raising monoamines. Antidepressants raise levels quickly but act after weeks, so receptor adaptation and other changes are also involved.
- **Neuroendocrine**: overactive hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, high cortisol.
- **Neurotrophic**: reduced BDNF and shrinkage of hippocampus.
- Genetic tendency, stressful life events, chronic illness, drugs (corticosteroids, some antihypertensives).

Bipolar disorder: episodes of depression alternating with mania.

### Schizophrenia

A chronic psychotic disorder, usually starting in late teens or early adulthood, with disordered thinking and loss of contact with reality.

| Symptom group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Positive (added) | Hallucinations (mostly hearing voices), delusions (persecution), disorganised speech and behaviour |
| Negative (lost) | Flat emotion, poverty of speech, lack of motivation, social withdrawal |
| Cognitive | Poor attention, memory and planning |

**Pathophysiology**
- **Dopamine hypothesis**: excess dopamine (D2) activity in the **mesolimbic** pathway → positive symptoms; reduced dopamine in the **mesocortical** pathway → negative and cognitive symptoms. Supported by amphetamines causing psychosis and antipsychotics blocking D2 receptors.
- **Glutamate hypothesis**: reduced NMDA receptor function (phencyclidine and ketamine mimic schizophrenia).
- Genetic factors, birth complications, cannabis use, enlarged ventricles on brain scans.

### Alzheimer's disease

The most common cause of **dementia** (progressive loss of memory and thinking severe enough to affect daily life), usually after 65 years.

**Pathology**
- **Extracellular amyloid (senile) plaques** of β-amyloid protein, from abnormal cleavage of amyloid precursor protein.
- **Intracellular neurofibrillary tangles** of hyperphosphorylated **tau** protein.
- Loss of neurons and synapses, especially in the hippocampus and cortex → brain atrophy, enlarged ventricles.
- **Cholinergic deficit**: loss of acetylcholine neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert (basis of cholinesterase-inhibitor therapy); excess glutamate activity.

**Risk factors**: age, family history, apolipoprotein E ε4 allele, Down syndrome, head injury, vascular risk factors.

**Features**: early loss of recent memory, repeating questions, losing things; later disorientation, language difficulty, poor judgement, personality change, wandering; finally total dependence and death from infection.

## 3.15 Peptic ulcer

**Definition.** A break in the mucosa of the stomach or duodenum, extending through the muscularis mucosae, exposed to acid and pepsin. Most common in the first part of the duodenum and the lesser curvature of the stomach.

### Pathogenesis: imbalance of aggressive and protective factors

| Aggressive factors | Protective factors |
| --- | --- |
| Hydrochloric acid, pepsin | Mucus–bicarbonate layer |
| ***Helicobacter pylori*** infection (most common cause) | Prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2): mucus, bicarbonate, blood flow |
| NSAIDs and aspirin (block COX → less protective prostaglandin) | Good mucosal blood flow |
| Smoking, alcohol, stress, corticosteroids with NSAIDs | Rapid cell renewal, tight junctions |
| Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrin-secreting tumour, huge acid output) | |

*H. pylori* is a spiral, gram-negative bacterium that lives under the mucus; its **urease** makes ammonia that neutralises acid around it, and its toxins and the inflammation they cause damage the mucosa and raise gastrin and acid secretion.

### Gastric versus duodenal ulcer

| Feature | Gastric ulcer | Duodenal ulcer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frequency | Less common | More common |
| Acid output | Normal or low | Often high |
| Pain timing | Soon after meals; food may worsen | 2–3 hours after meals and at night; relieved by food or antacids |
| Weight | Weight loss (fear of eating) | Weight may increase |
| Cancer risk | Must be biopsied to exclude cancer | Malignant change very rare |

**Symptoms**: burning or gnawing upper abdominal (epigastric) pain, heartburn, nausea, bloating; may be silent with NSAIDs.

**Complications**: bleeding (vomiting blood — haematemesis; black tarry stools — melaena), perforation (sudden severe pain, peritonitis), gastric outlet obstruction (vomiting), malignancy (gastric).

**Diagnosis**: endoscopy with biopsy; *H. pylori* tests (urea breath test, stool antigen, rapid urease test on biopsy).

## Remember

- Anaemia: Hb below 13 (men), 12 (women), 11 (pregnancy) g/dL. Microcytic = iron deficiency, thalassaemia; macrocytic = B12, folate.
- Iron deficiency: koilonychia, pica, low ferritin; usual cause is chronic blood loss.
- B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia) gives nerve damage; folate does not. Hypersegmented neutrophils in both.
- Sickle cell: Glu → Val at β6; sickling causes vaso-occlusive crises and haemolysis. Thalassaemia: reduced globin chain synthesis, iron overload.
- Haemophilia A = factor VIII, B = factor IX, both X-linked recessive; haemarthrosis; prolonged aPTT.
- Diabetes: FPG ≥ 126, 2-h ≥ 200, HbA1c ≥ 6.5%. Type 1 autoimmune, ketoacidosis; type 2 insulin resistance, obesity.
- Graves' = TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies; Hashimoto's = hypothyroidism; cretinism in infants.
- Parkinson's: nigral dopamine loss, Lewy bodies; tremor, rigidity, akinesia, postural instability.
- Stroke: 80–85% ischaemic; hypertension is the main risk factor; penumbra can be saved.
- Depression: monoamine deficit; schizophrenia: mesolimbic dopamine excess; Alzheimer's: amyloid plaques, tau tangles, ACh loss.
- Peptic ulcer: H. pylori and NSAIDs are the main causes; duodenal pain is relieved by food.

# Unit 4: Bowel and liver diseases, bone and joint diseases, principles of cancer

This unit covers inflammatory bowel disease, jaundice, viral hepatitis and alcoholic liver disease; rheumatoid arthritis, osteoporosis and gout; and the general principles of cancer. Comparison tables (Crohn's vs ulcerative colitis, types of jaundice, hepatitis viruses, benign vs malignant tumours) are easy marks, and cancer pathogenesis is a common long question.

## 4.1 Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)

**Definition.** Chronic, relapsing, immune-mediated inflammation of the intestine that is not caused by a known infection. The two main forms are **Crohn's disease** and **ulcerative colitis**.

### Aetiology and pathogenesis

The exact cause is unknown. Current view:

```text
Genetic susceptibility (e.g. NOD2 gene in Crohn's, family history)
        +
Abnormal gut bacteria (dysbiosis) and a leaky epithelial barrier
        +
Environmental triggers (smoking worsens Crohn's, Western diet, infections, NSAIDs)
        ↓
Inappropriate, persistent immune response (Th1/Th17 in Crohn's, Th2-like in UC)
→ TNF-α, IL-12, IL-23 and other cytokines → chronic inflammation and tissue damage
```

Young adults (15–30 years) are most often affected.

### Crohn's disease versus ulcerative colitis

| Feature | Crohn's disease | Ulcerative colitis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Site | Any part of the gut from mouth to anus; terminal ileum most common | Colon only; always starts at the **rectum** and spreads upwards |
| Distribution | **Skip lesions** (patchy, normal bowel between) | **Continuous** |
| Depth | **Transmural** (full thickness) | Mucosa and submucosa only |
| Gross look | Cobblestone mucosa, deep fissuring ulcers, thick wall, "string sign" narrowing | Broad shallow ulcers, pseudopolyps, loss of folds ("lead-pipe" colon) |
| Microscopy | Non-caseating **granulomas** | Crypt abscesses, no granulomas |
| Fistulae, strictures | Common | Rare |
| Bleeding per rectum | Less common | Common — bloody diarrhoea with mucus |
| Smoking | Worsens | Seems protective |
| Cancer risk | Raised | Raised more (long-standing pancolitis) |
| Special complication | Malabsorption (B12 in ileal disease), perianal disease, obstruction | **Toxic megacolon**, severe haemorrhage |

**Common symptoms**: chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain, weight loss, fever, tiredness, anaemia; Crohn's often presents with right lower abdominal pain, UC with frequent bloody stools and urgency.

**Extra-intestinal features** (both): arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, primary sclerosing cholangitis (mainly UC), gallstones and kidney stones (Crohn's).

## 4.2 Jaundice

**Definition.** Yellow colour of the skin, sclera and mucous membranes due to a raised **bilirubin** in the blood. Normal serum bilirubin is below about 1 mg/dL; jaundice becomes visible at about 2–3 mg/dL. The sclera shows it first.

### Bilirubin metabolism

```text
Old red cells (spleen) → haemoglobin → haem → biliverdin → UNCONJUGATED bilirubin
   (fat-soluble, carried on albumin, NOT in urine)
        ↓ liver uptake
   Conjugation with glucuronic acid (enzyme UDP-glucuronyl transferase)
        ↓
   CONJUGATED bilirubin (water-soluble) → bile → intestine
        ↓ bacteria
   Urobilinogen → stercobilin (brown stool colour)
              → part reabsorbed → urobilinogen in urine
```

### Types of jaundice

| Feature | Pre-hepatic (haemolytic) | Hepatic (hepatocellular) | Post-hepatic (obstructive, cholestatic) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cause | Excess breakdown of red cells: haemolytic anaemias, malaria, mismatched transfusion, neonatal jaundice | Liver cell damage: viral hepatitis, alcohol, drugs (paracetamol overdose, isoniazid, rifampicin), cirrhosis; Gilbert syndrome | Block to bile flow: gallstones in the common bile duct, cancer of the head of pancreas, biliary stricture; drug-induced cholestasis |
| Bilirubin raised | Unconjugated | Both | Conjugated |
| Urine bilirubin | Absent ("acholuric") | Present | Present (dark urine) |
| Urine urobilinogen | Increased | Variable | Absent (complete block) |
| Stool | Dark | Normal or pale | **Pale, clay-coloured** |
| Itching | No | Sometimes | Common (bile salts in skin) |
| Liver enzymes | Normal | High ALT, AST | High alkaline phosphatase and GGT |

**Neonatal (physiological) jaundice**: common in the first week because liver conjugation is immature and red cells break down fast. Very high unconjugated bilirubin can enter the newborn brain (**kernicterus**).

## 4.3 Viral hepatitis (A, B, C, D, E and the so-called F)

**Hepatitis** is inflammation of the liver. Viral hepatitis can be acute (less than 6 months) or chronic (more than 6 months).

| Virus | Type | Spread | Incubation (approx.) | Chronic infection | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A (HAV) | RNA, picornavirus | **Faeco-oral** (contaminated food and water) | 2–6 weeks | No | Children often mild; outbreaks; vaccine available |
| B (HBV) | **DNA**, hepadnavirus | **Blood, sexual, mother to child**, shared needles | 1–6 months | Yes — under about 5% of infected adults, but about 90% of infants infected at birth | Cirrhosis and liver cancer; vaccine available; markers HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs |
| C (HCV) | RNA, flavivirus | **Blood** (transfusion before screening, injecting drug use, unsafe injections), less often sexual | 2 weeks–6 months | Yes — the majority (about 70%) | Often silent for years; cirrhosis and liver cancer; no vaccine; curable with antivirals |
| D (HDV) | Defective RNA virus | Blood, sexual | — | Yes | **Needs HBV** (uses HBsAg coat): co-infection or superinfection; worsens hepatitis B |
| E (HEV) | RNA virus | **Faeco-oral** (water-borne epidemics, common in India) | 2–8 weeks | Rarely (only in the immunocompromised) | High death rate in **pregnant women** (fulminant hepatitis) |
| "F" | Not established | — | — | — | Proposed after some cases were not explained by A–E; the virus was never confirmed, so "hepatitis F" is not a recognised separate disease |

Easy memory: **A and E come through the bowel ("vowels → bowels")**; B, C, D come through blood and body fluids.

### Pathogenesis

Hepatitis viruses mostly do not kill liver cells directly; liver injury comes largely from the **host's immune response** (cytotoxic T cells attacking infected hepatocytes). A strong response clears the virus (acute hepatitis); a weak response lets the virus persist (chronic hepatitis).

### Clinical course of acute hepatitis

1. **Prodrome (pre-icteric)**: fever, malaise, loss of appetite, nausea, distaste for smoking, aching in the right upper abdomen.
2. **Icteric phase**: jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, tender enlarged liver; patient often feels better as jaundice appears.
3. **Recovery** over weeks.

**Outcomes**: full recovery; **fulminant hepatic failure** (encephalopathy, bleeding — rare); chronic hepatitis → **cirrhosis** → **hepatocellular carcinoma** (B, C, D); carrier state (B).

**Laboratory**: very high ALT and AST, raised bilirubin, viral markers (anti-HAV IgM, HBsAg, anti-HCV, anti-HEV IgM).

## 4.4 Alcoholic liver disease

Long-term heavy alcohol intake damages the liver in three overlapping stages.

```text
Heavy drinking
   ↓
1. FATTY LIVER (steatosis) – fat in liver cells; enlarged, yellow liver;
   usually no symptoms; REVERSIBLE if drinking stops
   ↓
2. ALCOHOLIC HEPATITIS – liver cell swelling and necrosis, neutrophils,
   Mallory bodies; fever, jaundice, tender liver; can be fatal
   ↓
3. ALCOHOLIC CIRRHOSIS – fibrous bands + regenerating nodules
   (micronodular); IRREVERSIBLE
```

### Pathogenesis

- Alcohol is oxidised by alcohol dehydrogenase (and CYP2E1 in heavy drinkers) to **acetaldehyde**, which is toxic: it binds proteins, damages microtubules and mitochondria.
- Oxidation produces excess **NADH**, which favours fat synthesis and blocks fatty acid oxidation → fatty liver.
- CYP2E1 activity generates **free radicals** (oxidative stress).
- Gut bacterial endotoxin reaches the liver → Kupffer cells release TNF-α → inflammation.
- Stellate (Ito) cells become activated and lay down collagen → fibrosis.
- Poor diet adds to the damage.

### Complications of cirrhosis (any cause)

| Problem | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Portal hypertension | Fibrosis blocks portal flow → oesophageal varices (bleeding, haematemesis), splenomegaly, caput medusae |
| Ascites and oedema | Portal hypertension + low albumin + salt retention (RAAS) |
| Hepatic encephalopathy | Ammonia and other toxins not cleared: confusion, flapping tremor, coma |
| Bleeding tendency | Fewer clotting factors (raised PT) and low platelets |
| Jaundice | Failing liver cells |
| Hormonal changes | Less oestrogen breakdown: gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, spider naevi, palmar erythema |
| Hepatorenal syndrome, infections | Kidney failure, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis |
| Hepatocellular carcinoma | Risk raised in cirrhosis |

**Drug relevance**: impaired drug metabolism and low albumin → dose adjustment; avoid hepatotoxic drugs and sedatives.

## 4.5 Rheumatoid arthritis

**Definition.** A chronic, systemic, **autoimmune** inflammatory disease mainly affecting the synovium of joints, giving **symmetrical polyarthritis** of small joints, which can destroy cartilage and bone. Women are affected about three times more than men, usually between 30 and 50 years.

### Pathogenesis

```text
Genetic susceptibility (HLA-DR4, shared epitope) + trigger (smoking, infection?)
   ↓ citrullination of proteins → loss of tolerance
Autoreactive CD4 T cells and B cells → autoantibodies:
   rheumatoid factor (IgM against Fc of IgG), anti-CCP (anti-citrullinated protein)
   ↓ cytokines TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6
Synovium becomes inflamed, thick and proliferates = PANNUS
   (granulation tissue with lymphocytes, plasma cells, new vessels)
   ↓ pannus grows over and erodes cartilage and bone (osteoclast activation)
Joint destruction → fibrous / bony ankylosis and deformity
```

### Clinical features

- Pain, swelling and warmth of small joints of hands (MCP, PIP) and feet, wrists, knees — **symmetrical**; distal interphalangeal joints usually spared.
- **Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour**, improving with use.
- Deformities: **ulnar deviation** of fingers, **swan-neck** and **boutonnière** deformities, Z-thumb.
- Systemic: fatigue, low fever, weight loss, anaemia of chronic disease.
- Extra-articular: rheumatoid nodules (elbows), dry eyes and mouth (Sjögren's), lung fibrosis, pericarditis, vasculitis, raised cardiovascular risk, carpal tunnel syndrome.
- Tests: raised ESR and CRP, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP (more specific), X-ray erosions near joint margins.

**RA vs osteoarthritis**: RA — autoimmune inflammation, small joints, symmetrical, long morning stiffness, systemic; OA — "wear and tear" of cartilage, weight-bearing joints (knee, hip) and DIP joints, stiffness under 30 minutes, worse with use, no systemic illness.

## 4.6 Osteoporosis

**Definition.** A systemic skeletal disease with **low bone mass** and **deterioration of bone micro-architecture**, giving fragile bones and a high risk of fracture. The bone that is present is normally mineralised (compare osteomalacia, where mineralisation is poor). WHO definition by DEXA scan: bone mineral density **T-score of −2.5 or lower**; −1 to −2.5 = osteopenia.

### Pathogenesis

Bone is constantly remodelled: **osteoclasts** remove bone and **osteoblasts** form it. Osteoporosis results when resorption exceeds formation.

| Type | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| Primary type I (postmenopausal) | Loss of oestrogen after menopause → more RANKL, more osteoclast activity → rapid loss of trabecular bone → vertebral and wrist fractures |
| Primary type II (senile) | Ageing in both sexes: fewer osteoblasts, less calcium absorption, less vitamin D → loss of cortical and trabecular bone → hip fractures |
| Secondary | Long-term **corticosteroids** (most common drug cause), heparin, anticonvulsants, excess thyroxine; hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, Cushing's syndrome, hypogonadism, chronic kidney and liver disease, rheumatoid arthritis, malabsorption, immobilisation |

**Risk factors**: female sex, age, early menopause, thin build, family history, low calcium and vitamin D intake, lack of exercise, smoking, alcohol.

**Features**: a "silent disease" until fracture. Fractures of vertebrae (loss of height, kyphosis or "dowager's hump", back pain), wrist (Colles' fracture), and hip (neck of femur — high disability and death in the elderly).

## 4.7 Gout

**Definition.** A metabolic disease in which raised serum **uric acid** (hyperuricaemia) leads to deposition of **monosodium urate crystals** in and around joints, causing very painful attacks of arthritis, and in tissues and kidneys. Uric acid is the end product of **purine** metabolism (xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid). Blood becomes saturated with urate above about 6.8 mg/dL.

### Causes of hyperuricaemia

| Over-production (about 10%) | Under-excretion by the kidney (about 90%) |
| --- | --- |
| High-purine diet (red meat, organ meat, seafood), alcohol (beer), fructose drinks | Kidney disease |
| Rapid cell turnover: leukaemia, lymphoma, cancer chemotherapy (tumour lysis), psoriasis | Drugs: thiazide and loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, ciclosporin |
| Enzyme defects (Lesch–Nyhan syndrome, HGPRT deficiency) | Lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis (compete for excretion), obesity, hypertension |

### Pathogenesis of an acute attack

```text
Urate crystals form in the joint (cool, distal joints; trauma, alcohol, dehydration)
→ crystals are taken up by neutrophils and macrophages
→ NLRP3 inflammasome → IL-1β → intense acute inflammation
→ hot, red, swollen, exquisitely painful joint
```

### Clinical stages

1. **Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia** — most people never get gout.
2. **Acute gouty arthritis** — sudden severe pain, often at night, usually in **one joint**: classically the **first metatarsophalangeal joint (big toe) = podagra**; also ankle, knee. Settles in days to two weeks.
3. **Intercritical period** — free intervals between attacks.
4. **Chronic tophaceous gout** — **tophi** (chalky urate deposits) in ear helix, around joints, tendons; joint destruction.

**Kidney effects**: uric acid stones, urate nephropathy.

**Diagnosis**: needle-shaped, **negatively birefringent** crystals in joint fluid under polarised light (pseudogout crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent). Serum uric acid can be normal during an attack.

## 4.8 Principles of cancer

**Neoplasm (tumour)**: an abnormal mass of tissue whose growth is excessive, uncoordinated with normal tissue, and continues after the stimulus stops. **Cancer** is the common term for malignant neoplasms. **Oncology** is the study of tumours.

### Classification

**By behaviour**

| Feature | Benign tumour | Malignant tumour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Growth rate | Slow | Usually fast |
| Capsule | Often present | Absent |
| Spread | Expands, pushes tissue aside | **Invades** surrounding tissue |
| Metastasis | Never | Common |
| Differentiation | Well differentiated, like the parent tissue | Poorly differentiated to undifferentiated (anaplasia) |
| Cells | Uniform | Pleomorphic, large dark nuclei, many abnormal mitoses |
| Recurrence after removal | Rare | Common |
| Effect on patient | Usually by pressure or hormones | Can kill (cachexia, organ failure) |

**By tissue of origin (naming)**

| Origin | Benign | Malignant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Covering / glandular epithelium | Papilloma, adenoma | **Carcinoma** (squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma) |
| Connective tissue (mesenchyme) | Lipoma, fibroma, osteoma, chondroma, leiomyoma | **Sarcoma** (liposarcoma, osteosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma) |
| Blood-forming cells | — | Leukaemia, lymphoma, myeloma |
| Melanocytes | Naevus (mole) | Melanoma |
| Germ cells | Mature teratoma | Seminoma, malignant teratoma |
| Embryonic tissue | — | Blastomas (retinoblastoma, neuroblastoma, Wilms' tumour) |

Note: melanoma, lymphoma and seminoma are malignant even though the names end in "-oma".

### Aetiology (causes and risk factors)

| Group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Chemical carcinogens | Tobacco smoke (lung, mouth, bladder), gutka and betel quid (oral cancer — very common in India), polycyclic hydrocarbons, aromatic amines (bladder), aflatoxin (liver), asbestos (mesothelioma), benzene (leukaemia), alkylating drugs (cyclophosphamide) |
| Radiation | UV light (skin cancer, melanoma), ionising radiation (leukaemia, thyroid cancer) |
| Viruses (oncogenic) | Human papillomavirus (cervical cancer), hepatitis B and C (liver cancer), Epstein–Barr virus (Burkitt's lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma), HTLV-1 (T-cell leukaemia), HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma) |
| Bacteria | *Helicobacter pylori* (gastric cancer, gastric lymphoma) |
| Hormones | Oestrogen (endometrium, breast) |
| Heredity | BRCA1/BRCA2 (breast, ovary), RB gene (retinoblastoma), APC (familial polyposis colon cancer) |
| Others | Age, obesity, alcohol, chronic inflammation (ulcerative colitis), immunosuppression |

### Pathogenesis (molecular basis)

Cancer is a **genetic disease of cells**: non-lethal damage to DNA accumulates in a single cell, which then grows into a clone (monoclonal origin). Four classes of genes are targets:

| Gene class | Normal role | In cancer | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Proto-oncogenes → **oncogenes** | Promote normal growth | Gain-of-function mutation → constant "accelerator" | RAS, MYC, HER2 (ERBB2), BCR-ABL |
| **Tumour suppressor genes** | Brake on cell growth | Loss-of-function (both copies — Knudson's "two-hit" idea) → "brakes fail" | p53 ("guardian of the genome"), RB, APC, BRCA1/2 |
| Apoptosis-regulating genes | Remove damaged cells | Anti-apoptotic genes overactive → damaged cells survive | BCL-2 over-expression |
| DNA repair genes | Fix DNA errors | Defective repair → mutations pile up | Mismatch repair genes, BRCA |

```text
Carcinogen / virus / radiation / inherited mutation
        ↓
DNA damage escapes repair
        ↓
Activation of oncogenes + loss of tumour suppressors + loss of apoptosis
        ↓
Clonal growth → more mutations (tumour progression)
        ↓
Hallmarks gained: self-sufficient growth signals, ignoring growth inhibitors,
escape from apoptosis, unlimited replication (telomerase),
new blood vessels (angiogenesis, VEGF), invasion and metastasis,
altered metabolism (Warburg effect), escape from immune attack
```

**Multistep carcinogenesis**: initiation (irreversible DNA damage) → promotion (growth of initiated cells by promoters such as hormones, phorbol esters) → progression (more mutations, invasion).

### Invasion and metastasis

Tumour cells loosen from each other (loss of E-cadherin), attach to and digest the basement membrane (metalloproteinases), migrate, enter vessels, survive in blood, exit at a distant site and grow there.

| Route | Typical of | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lymphatic | Carcinomas | Breast cancer → axillary nodes |
| Blood (haematogenous) | Sarcomas, also many carcinomas | Liver and lungs are common sites; bone (prostate, breast) |
| Seeding of body cavities (transcoelomic) | | Ovarian cancer across the peritoneum |

**Grading** (how differentiated the cells look) and **staging** (how far it has spread — TNM: Tumour size, Node involvement, Metastasis) guide treatment and prognosis; stage matters more.

**Effects on the patient**: local pressure and obstruction, bleeding, infection, pain, **cachexia** (wasting), paraneoplastic syndromes (hormone-like effects, e.g. hypercalcaemia), anaemia.

## Remember

- Crohn's: mouth-to-anus, skip lesions, transmural, granulomas, fistulae. UC: rectum upwards, continuous, mucosal, crypt abscesses, bloody diarrhoea, toxic megacolon.
- Jaundice visible above about 2–3 mg/dL bilirubin. Haemolytic = unconjugated, no bilirubin in urine; obstructive = conjugated, dark urine, pale stools, itching, high ALP.
- Hepatitis A and E faeco-oral, no chronic state (E dangerous in pregnancy); B (DNA), C, D blood-borne, can become chronic; D needs B; "F" is not an established virus.
- Alcoholic liver disease: fatty liver → alcoholic hepatitis (Mallory bodies) → cirrhosis; acetaldehyde, NADH, free radicals.
- RA: autoimmune, symmetrical small joints, pannus, RF and anti-CCP, morning stiffness > 1 h, ulnar deviation.
- Osteoporosis: T-score ≤ −2.5; postmenopausal (oestrogen loss) and senile; steroids are the main drug cause.
- Gout: urate crystals (needle, negatively birefringent), podagra, tophi; diuretics and alcohol raise uric acid.
- Benign vs malignant: invasion and metastasis decide. Carcinoma = epithelial, sarcoma = mesenchymal.
- Cancer genes: oncogenes (RAS, MYC), tumour suppressors (p53, RB), apoptosis (BCL-2), DNA repair.
